semin-durr:3-3.t: [Translator's note: the source entry begins here without restating the Quranic words; it concerns {الرحمن الرحيم} in this ayah.] A naʿt (adjective) or a badal (substitute). They have also been read in the accusative and in the nominative, and the justification of that is what was mentioned under {رَبِّ العالمين}. The discussion of their derivation has already come under the Basmala, which makes it unnecessary to repeat it.

semin-durr:6-6.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {اهدنا الصراط} to the end of it: اهْدِ is an imperative form whose meaning is supplication (duʿāʾ). This form occurs with many meanings which the legal theorists (al-uṣūliyyūn) have mentioned. One of them said: if the form افعَلْ comes from a superior to an inferior it is called a command (amr); in the reverse case, a supplication (duʿāʾ); and from an equal, a request (iltimās). Its fāʿil (agent) is obligatorily latent (mustatir), for the reason given earlier, i.e. "guide, You". And نا is the first mafʿūl bihi (direct object); it is an attached pronoun used for the speaker together with others, or for one who speaks of himself in the plural of majesty. It is used in the position of the nominative, the accusative and the genitive with a single form, as in: قُمنَا, ضرَبَنَا زيدٌ and مَرَّ بنا, and no other pronoun shares this peculiarity with it. Some people have claimed that the yāʾ is likewise; you say: أكرمَنَي, مرِّ بي and أنت تقومين يا هند; the yāʾ in the first example is in the position of the accusative, in the second in the position of the genitive, and in the third in the position of the nominative. This is worthless, because the yāʾ in the nominative is not the same yāʾ as the one in the accusative and the genitive: the latter is for the speaker, while this one is for the feminine addressee. It has also been said: rather, the word «هُمْ» shares it; you say: هم نائمون, ضربَهم and مررت بهم, so «هم» is in the position of the nominative, the accusative and the genitive with a single form, and it is for the absent (third person plural) in every case. Although this is closer than the first, in the nominative it is a detached pronoun, while in the accusative and genitive it is an attached pronoun, so the two differ — unlike «نا», whose meaning does not differ and which is an attached pronoun in all three cases. [Translator's note: the source prints «ن» for the pronoun نا in two places; rendered here as نا.]
والصراطَ is the second mafʿūl bihi, and المستقيمَ is its naʿt (adjective); it has followed it in four of the ten things mentioned [Translator's note: i.e. the ten features of agreement between an adjective and its noun — case, definiteness, gender, number, etc.].
The basic usage of «هَدَى» is that it is transitive to the first object by itself and to the second by a preposition, which is either إلى or the lām, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: {وَإِنَّكَ لتهدي إلى صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ} [al-Shūrā: 52] and {يِهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ} [al-Isrāʾ: 9]. Then latitude is taken with it, the preposition is dropped, and it becomes transitive by itself. So the underlying form of اهدنا الصراط is اهدنا للصراط or إلى الصراطِ, and then [the preposition] was dropped. [Translator's note: the source repeats the word الحرفُ by a printing error.]
The imperative, according to the Basrans, is indeclinable (mabnī), and according to the Kufans it is declinable (muʿrab). They claim that in a word like «اضرب» the underlying form is لِتَضْرِب, with the lām of command; then the jussive-governing particle was dropped, followed by the imperfect prefix, and the connecting hamza (hamzat al-waṣl) was brought in because one cannot begin with a vowelless letter. This is something there is no need for, and refuting them has a more fitting place.
The pattern of اهْدِ is افْعِ: its final radical, the yāʾ, has been dropped, treating the imperative like the jussive (majzūm), and in the jussive the final radical is dropped when it is a weak letter.
Al-hidāya (guidance) is directing (irshād), or indicating (dalāla), or going ahead (taqaddum); from this come هَوادِي الخيل ("the leaders of the horses"), because they go ahead. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
67 - فَأَلْحَقَه بالهاديات ودونَه ... جواحِرُها في صَرَّةٍ لم تَزَيًّلِ
(He brought him up with the leading ones [of the herd], while the laggards were left behind him in a close pack that did not scatter.)
Or making clear (tabyīn), as in: {وَأَمَّا ثَمُودُ فَهَدَيْنَاهُمْ} [Fuṣṣilat: 17], i.e. We made clear to them; or inspiration (ilhām), as in: {أعطى كُلَّ شَيءٍ خَلْقَهُ ثُمَّ هدى} [Ṭā Hā: 50], i.e. He inspired it toward what is good for it; or calling (duʿāʾ), as in the words of Allah the Exalted: {وَلِكُلِّ قَوْمٍ هَادٍ} [al-Raʿd: 7], i.e. a caller. It has also been said that it is inclining (mayl), and from it is {إِنَّا هُدْنَآ إِلَيْكَ} [al-Aʿrāf: 56], the meaning being: incline our hearts to You. This is a mistake, for that is a different root, from هادَ يَهُود. [Translator's note: the reference as printed is al-Aʿrāf: 56; the verse is al-Aʿrāf 7:156.] Al-Rāghib said: "Hidāya is guidance with gentleness; from it come al-hadiyya (the gift) and هوادي الوحش, i.e. the foremost wild animals that lead others. Guidance in the sense of indicating is specified with هَدَيتُ, and that in the sense of giving with أَهْديت."
Al-ṣirāṭ is the easy-to-travel road; some do not restrict it to being easy to travel. [The poet] said:
68 - فَضَلَّ عن نَهْج الصراطِ الواضِحِ ...
(So he strayed from the course of the clear road.)
And similarly:
69 - أميرُ المؤمنين على صِراطٍ ... إذا اعْوَجَّ المَوارِدُ مستقيمِ
(The Commander of the Faithful is on a straight road when the watering-paths go crooked.)
Another said:
70 - شَحَنَّا أرضَهم بالخيلِ حتى ... تَرَكْناهُمْ أَذَلَّ من الصِّراطِ
(We filled their land with horses until we left them more trodden-down than the road.)
i.e. the road. It is derived from al-sirṭ, which is swallowing: either because the one travelling it swallows it up, or because it swallows up the one who travels it. Do you not see their saying: "The one who knows a land kills it, and a land kills the one ignorant of it"? On these two considerations Abū Tammām said:
71 - رَعَتْه الفيافي بعدما كان حِقْبةً ... رعاها وماءُ المُزْنِ يَنْهَلُّ ساكِبُهْ
(The deserts grazed upon him after he had for a long time grazed upon them, while the water of the rain-clouds poured down.)
On this basis the road was called لَقَم and مُلْتَقِم, because it gobbles up the one travelling it, or the one travelling it gobbles it up.
Its original letter is the sīn, and Qunbul read it so wherever it occurs. It was changed into ṣād only because of the elevated letter (ḥarf al-istiʿlāʾ) [i.e. the ṭāʾ], and changing it into ṣād is regular in this circumstance, as in صَقَر for سَقَر, صُلْح for سُلْح, إصْبَع for اسبَع and مُصَيْطِر for مُسَيْطر, because of the closeness between the two.
The ṣād in الصراط and the like may be given a tinge of zāy (ishmām), and Khalaf read it so wherever it occurs, and Khallād only in the first occurrence; it may also be read as a pure zāy. In the Muṣḥaf it is written only with ṣād, despite their differing readings of it, as stated above.
Al-ṣirāṭ is treated as masculine and feminine: the masculine is the dialect of Tamīm and the feminine the dialect of the Ḥijāz. If it is used as masculine, its plural of paucity is أَفْعِلة and its plural of multitude فُعُل, as in حِمار, أَحْمِرة and حُمُر; if it is used as feminine, its analogical plural is أَفْعُل, as in ذِراع and أَذْرُع. Al-mustaqīm is the active participle of استقام in the sense of the bare verb; its meaning is "level, without crookedness". Its underlying form is مُسْتَقْوِم, then it underwent the same weak-letter change (iʿlāl) as نَسْتعين. The full discussion of its root will come at the words of Allah the Exalted: {يُقِيمُونَ الصلاة}.

semin-durr:5-5.t:
«إياك» is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object) placed before «نَعْبُدُ»; it was put first for restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ), and it must be a detached pronoun. They disagreed about it: is it of the category of overt nouns or of pronouns? The majority hold that it is a pronoun, while al-Zajjāj said: "It is an overt noun." The arguments for preferring each of the two views are mentioned in the books of grammar.
Those who say it is a pronoun disagreed about it in four views. The first: that the whole of it is the pronoun. The second: that «إيَّا» alone is the pronoun, and what follows it is a noun in the position of muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), making clear what is intended by it — first person, third person or second person. The third: that «إيَّا» alone is the pronoun, and what follows it are particles that make clear what is intended by it. The fourth: that «إيَّا» is a support (ʿimād), and what follows it is the pronoun. Its annexation to an overt noun occurs anomalously in their saying: «إذا بلغ الرجلُ الستين فإياه وإيَّا الشَوابِّ» ("When a man reaches sixty, let him beware of young women"), with «إيا» annexed to الشَوابِّ; and this supports the view of whoever makes the kāf, the hāʾ and the yāʾ in the position of the genitive when you say: إياك, إياه, إياي.
Some grammarians went far astray and assigned it a derivation, then said: is it derived from «أَوّ», as in the poet's words:
59 - فَأَوِّ لذِكْراها إذا ما ذَكَرْتُها ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(So: ah! at the memory of her whenever I remember her …)
or from «آية», as in his words:
60 - لم يُبْقِ هذا الدهرُ من آيائِهِ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(This age has left nothing of its signs …)
And is its pattern إفْعَل, or فَعيل, or فَعُول, which morphological change then turned into the form إيَّا? What this speaker mentioned brings no benefit; besides, morphology and derivation do not enter into what is deeply rooted in indeclinability.
There are several dialectal forms of it: the best known is with kasra on the hamza and a doubled yāʾ; among them also is fatḥa on the hamza, and changing it into hāʾ, with the yāʾ doubled or undoubled. The poet said:
61 - فَهِيَّاك والأمرَ الذي إنْ توسَّعَتْ ... مَواردُه ضاقَتْ عليك مصادِرُهْ
(So beware of an affair whose entrances, if they widen, will make its exits narrow upon you.)
[And one of them said: إياك with an undoubled yāʾ is to be avoided], because it would become "Your sun we worship", since إياة of the sun is its light, with kasra on the hamza, and it may take fatḥa. It has also been said: it is to the sun what the halo is to the moon. If you drop the tāʾ you lengthen it. [The poet] said:
62 - سَقَتْه إياةُ الشمسِ إلاَّ لِثاتِه ... أُسِفَّ فلم تَكْدِمْ عليه بإثْمِدِ
(The light of the sun watered it [i.e. made it bright], except for its gums, which were dusted with antimony, and it did not bite upon it.)
Some of these forms have been read as anomalous readings (shādhdh). Pronouns have a long chapter and a wide division which this book cannot bear; only what suits it will come in its course.
And نعبُدُ is an imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ) because it is free of any accusative-governing or jussive-governing particle; it has also been said: because it occupies the place of a noun, and this is the view of the Basrans. The meaning of al-muḍāriʿ is "the resembling one", meaning that it resembles the noun in its vowelled and vowelless letters and in the number of its letters — do you not see that ضارب has the same measure as يَضْرب in what I have mentioned to you? — and in that it is general and becomes specific with respect to times, just as the noun is general and becomes specific with respect to persons. Its fāʿil (agent) is obligatorily latent (mustatir), for the reason given under the Istiʿādha.
Al-ʿibāda (worship) is the utmost self-abasement, and none deserves it except the one who has the utmost bounty, and He is the Creator, Exalted is He. So it is more far-reaching than al-ʿubūdiyya, because al-ʿubūdiyya is the display of self-abasement. One says طريق مُعَبَّد, i.e. a road made level by treading. Ṭarafa said:
63 - تباري عِتاقاً ناجِياتٍ وَأَتْبَعَتْ ... وَظِيفاً وظيفاً فوقَ مَوْرٍ مُعَبَّدِ
(She vies with swift, noble she-camels, placing foot after foot upon a well-trodden road.)
From it comes al-ʿabd (the slave), because of his lowliness, and بعيرٌ مُعَبَّد, i.e. a camel made docile [Translator's note: literally "abased"] by being smeared with tar.
It has also been said: al-ʿibāda is devoting oneself exclusively (al-tajarrud). One says عَبَدْت الله only without doubling, and عَبَّدْتُ الرجلَ only with doubling, i.e. I subdued him or took him as a slave.
In the words of Allah the Exalted {إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ} there is iltifāt (a shift of person) from the third person to the second person, for had the speech run according to its basic pattern, it would have been said: الحمد لله, and then: إياه نعبدُ. [Translator's note: the source prints «الحمد الله», evidently a misprint for الحمد لله.] Iltifāt is a kind of eloquence. Among the instances of iltifāt — though it is the reverse of this — are the words of Allah the Exalted: {حتى إِذَا كُنتُمْ فِي الفلك وَجَرَيْنَ بِهِم} [Yūnus: 22], and He did not say: بكم. Imruʾ al-Qays made three shifts of person in his words:
64 - تطاوَلَ ليلُكَ بالإِثمِدِ ... وبات الخَليُّ ولم تَرْقُدِ
وباتَ وباتَتْ له ليلَةٌ ... كليلة ذي العائِرِ الأرْمَدِ
وذلك من نبأٍ جاءني ... وخُبِّرْتُه عن أَبِي الأسودِ
(Your night has grown long at al-Ithmid, while the carefree one slept and you did not sleep; / And he passed the night, and a night passed for him like the night of one with a mote in his inflamed eye; / And that was because of news that came to me, and I was told it about Abū al-Aswad.)
Someone faulted al-Zamakhsharī for making these three shifts, and said: rather they are two shifts. The first is the departure from the second person with which it opens in his words «ليلُك» to the third person in his words «وباتَتْ له ليلةٌ»; the second is the departure from this third person to the first person in his words «من نبأٍ جاءني وخُبِّرْتُه». The answer is that his first words, «تطاول ليلُك», contain a shift of person, because the basic form of the speech would have been to say: تطاول ليلي, since he himself is the one meant. So he shifted from the position of the speaker to that of the addressee, then from the addressee to the third person, then from the third person to the speaker, which is the original.
It has been read as an anomalous reading: «إِيَّاكَ يُعْبَدُ», with the verb passive and in the third person. Its justification, despite its difficulty, is that it contains a borrowing (istiʿāra) and a shift of person. As for the borrowing: the accusative pronoun was borrowed for the nominative pronoun, the underlying form being أنت تُعْبَدُ ("You are worshipped"). This is common, as in their saying عساك, عساه and عساني according to one of the views, and in the words of another:
65 - يابنَ الزُّبير طالما عَصَيْكا ... وطالَمَا عَنِّيْتَنَا إِلَيكا
(O son of al-Zubayr, how long you have disobeyed, and how long you have made us toil toward you!)
The kāf in «عَصَيْكا» stands in for the tāʾ, the underlying form being عَصَيْتَ. As for the shift of person: this reader ought to have read إياك تُعْبَدُ, in the second person, but he shifted from the second person in «إيَّاك» to the third person in «يُعْبَدُ». This, however, is an unusual shift, because it is within a single sentence, unlike the shift mentioned before. An analogue of this shift is his words:
66 - أأنتَ الهلاليُّ الذي كنتَ مرةً ... سَمِعْنا به والأَرْحَبِيُّ المُغَلَّبُ
(Are you the Hilālī whom we once heard of, and the Arḥabī who was overcome?)
He said «به» after saying «أنت» and «كنت».
«إيَّاك» must come before its governing word, because the rule is that when the mafʿūl bihi is a pronoun which, if it came after its governing word, would have to be attached, it must be placed first. By their words "if it came after it, it would have to be attached" they guard against a case like «الدرهمَ إياه أعطيتُك», because if you put the pronoun after here, saying «الدرهمَ أعطيتُك إياه», attachment would not be obligatory, for a reason that will come; rather أعطيتُكه is also permitted.
The discussion of «إياك نَسْتعين» is like the discussion of «إياك نعبدُ». The wāw is a conjunction; it is one of those that associate [the two conjuncts] in case-inflection and in meaning, and it does not entail sequence according to the view of the majority, contrary to a group of the Kufans. It has rules peculiar to it which will come, if Allah the Exalted wills.
The underlying form of نَسْتعين is نَسْتَعْوِنُ, like نَسْتَخْرِجُ among sound verbs, because it is from al-ʿawn (help). The kasra was felt heavy on the wāw, so it was transferred to the vowelless letter before it; the wāw became vowelless after the transfer, the letter before it took kasra, and so it was changed into yāʾ. This is a regular rule, as in ميزان and مِيقات, which are from al-wazn and al-waqt.
The sīn in it means seeking: i.e. we seek help from You in worship. This is one of the meanings of the pattern استفعل, which has other meanings: taking as something, as in استعْبَدَه, i.e. he took him as a slave; transformation, as in استحْجَرَ الطين, i.e. the clay became stone, and from this is the saying: «إن البُغاثَ بأرضِنا تَسْتَنْسِر» ("Small birds in our land turn into eagles"), i.e. they turn into the qualities of eagles; finding a thing to have the meaning of what [the verb] is formed from, as in استعظَمه, i.e. he found it great; reckoning a thing so even if it is not, as in استحسنه; being the reflexive-resultative (muṭāwaʿa) of أَفْعَل, as in أَشْلاه فاستشلى; agreeing with it in meaning as well, as in أَبَلَّ المريضُ and استبلَّ ("the sick man recovered"); agreeing with تفعَّل, as in استكبرَ in the sense of تكبَّر; agreeing with افتَعَلَ, as in استعصمَ in the sense of اعتصم; dispensing with a bare form, as in استكفَّ and استحيى, for which no bare form is used because they suffice in its place; and dispensing with فَعَل, i.e. the bare form that is used, as in استرجع and استعانَ, i.e. he said "we belong to Allah and to Him we return", and he shaved his pubic hair (ʿāna). [Translator's note: the source glosses استرجع as «رَجَع»; translated as written. Also «نجو» before استكبر is a misprint for «نحو».]
It has been read «نِسْتعين», with kasra on the imperfect prefix. This is a dialect regularly applied to the imperfect prefixes, on condition that the prefix is not yāʾ, because of the heaviness of that — although some said يِيجَل as the imperfect of وَجِلَ, as if aiming to lighten the wāw into yāʾ, so he gave kasra to what precedes it so that it would change. And it has been read: {فإنهم يِيْلمونَ} [al-Nisāʾ: 104], which demolishes this exception; the verification of this will come in its place, if Allah the Exalted wills. [Other conditions are] that the imperfect be from a past verb whose middle radical has kasra, as in تِعْلم from عَلِمَ; or that it begin with a connecting hamza, as in نِسْتعين from استعان; or with a tāʾ of muṭāwaʿa, as in نِتَعلَّم from تَعَلَّم. So in يَضْرِبُ and يَقْتُل kasra on the imperfect prefix is not permitted, because the stated conditions are absent. Among the amusing things told is that Laylā al-Akhyaliyya was one of the people of this dialect. One day she came in to al-Ḥajjāj, while al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī was with him, and she mentioned the severe cold in her country. Al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī — knowing that she would fall into what he intended — said to her: "So what do you do? Do you not wrap yourselves up (تَكْتَنُون) in the severe cold?" She said: "Yes, we wrap ourselves up — نِكْتَني", giving kasra to the nūn. He said: "If I did that, I would have to take a ritual bath." [Translator's note: نِكْتَني as she pronounced it could be heard as نِكْتُ + نِي, with an obscene sense.] Al-Ḥajjāj laughed, and Laylā was embarrassed.
Al-istiʿāna is seeking help (ʿawn), which is backing and support. He put worship before seeking help because it is a means to seeking what one needs. He left both verbs — of worship and of seeking help — unrestricted, mentioning no object for them, so that they would cover everything by which worship is performed and everything for which help is sought; or the intended meaning is the occurrence of the action without regard to any object, as in {كُلوا واشربوا} [al-Baqara: 60], i.e. perform these two actions.

semin-durr:4-4.t:
[Translator's note: the entry concerns {مالك يوم الدين} / {مَلِك يوم الدين}; the source begins without restating the words.] It may also be a ṣifa (adjective) or a badal (substitute), even though a badal consisting of a derived word is rare. It is derived from al-malk, with fatḥa on the mīm, which is binding and tying. The poet said:
45 - مَلَكْتُ بها كَفِّي فَأَنْهَرْتُ فَتْقَها ... يَرَى قائمٌ مِنْ دونِها ما وراءها
(I tightened my hand on it [the spear] and widened its rent, so that one standing in front of it could see what is behind it.)
From it comes «إملاكُ العَروسِ» (the wedding of the bride), because it is a contract and a binding of marriage.
It has been read «مالِك», with alif. Al-Akhfash said: "One says مَلِكٌ بَيِّنُ المُلْكِ (a king of evident kingship), with ḍamma on the mīm, and مالكٌ بيِّنُ المَلْكِ/المِلْكِ (an owner of evident ownership), with fatḥa or kasra on the mīm"; and ḍamma on it has also been transmitted in this sense. It has been transmitted from the Arabs: «لي في هذا الوادي مَلْك ومُلْك ومِلْك» ("I have property in this valley"), with the first radical taking all three vowels. But what is well known is the distinction between the three words: the form with fatḥa is binding and tying; the form with ḍamma is subjugation and dominion over those from whom obedience can come, and it may be by right or otherwise; the form with kasra is dominion over those from whom obedience can come and those from whom it cannot, and it is only by right. So between the kasra form and the ḍamma form there is a relation of partial overlap (ʿumūm wa-khuṣūṣ min wajh). Al-Rāghib said: "Al-milk — i.e. with kasra — is like the genus for al-mulk — i.e. with ḍamma; so every milk — with kasra — is mulk, but not every mulk is milk." On this view the relation between them is one of absolute generality and specificity (ʿumūm wa-khuṣūṣ muṭlaq). [Translator's note: as printed, al-Rāghib's statement makes every milk a mulk; translated as written.] By this the difference between مَلِك and مالِك is known: مَلِك is taken from al-mulk, with ḍamma, and مالِك is taken from al-milk, with kasra. It has also been said: the difference between them is that al-malik is a name for everyone who possesses governance — either over himself, by having control of the reins of his faculties and turning them from their desires, or over himself and others, whether he actually takes charge of that or not.
Each party has preferred one of the two readings over the other with a preference that almost cancels the other reading. This is not acceptable, because both are mutawātir (mass-transmitted). What shows this is what is reported from Thaʿlab, that he said: ["When the case-inflection in the Quran differs] among the Seven, I do not prefer one inflection over another in the Quran; but when I go out to speech — the speech of people — I prefer the stronger." Abū ʿUmar al-Zāhid transmitted this in «al-Yawāqīt». Shaykh Shihāb al-Dīn Abū Shāma said: "The authors on the readings and on tafsīr have greatly multiplied preferences between these two readings, to the point that some of them go so far in this as almost to cancel the validity of the other reading. This is not praiseworthy after both readings have been established and the Lord, Exalted is He, has been validly described by both." Then he said: "I even pray with this one in one rakʿa and with that one in another rakʿa." He mentioned this at his words: «مَلِك يوم الدين ومالِك».
Let us mention some of the preferring arguments, drawing attention to the meaning of the word, not in the way they intended. Among the things by which the reading «مالك» was preferred: that it is more praising, because of the generality of what it is annexed to, since one says «مالِكُ الجِّن والإِنس والطير» ("Owner of the jinn, mankind and birds"); and they recited for that:
46 - سُبْحَانَ مَنْ عَنَتِ الوجوهُ لوجهِه ... مَلِكِ الملوكِ ومالِكِ العَفْوِ
(Glory be to Him to whose Face all faces are humbled, King of kings and Owner of pardon.)
And they say «فلانٌ مالكُ كذا» ("So-and-so is the owner of such-and-such") of one who owns it — unlike «مَلِك», which is annexed only to kings' subjects, as in «مَلِك العرب والعجم» ("king of the Arabs and non-Arabs") [Translator's note: the source reads «إلى غيرِ الملوك», literally "to other than kings"; and it prints «مِلك» for مَلِك]; and because an addition in the structure indicates an addition in meaning, as stated earlier under «الرحمن»; and because the reward of the one who recites it is greater than the reward of the one who recites «مَلِك».
Among the things by which the reading «مَلِك» was preferred is what al-Fārisī related from Ibn al-Sarrāj from one of them: that He has described Himself as the Owner of everything by His words {رَبِّ العالمين}, so there is no benefit in the reading of whoever read «مالك», because it is a repetition. Abū ʿAlī [al-Fārisī] said: "There is no proof in this, because there is much like it in the Revelation: the general is mentioned and then the particular, as in: {هُوَ الله الخالق البارىء المصور} [al-Ḥashr: 24]." Abū Ḥātim said: "«مالِك» is more far-reaching in praising the Creator, and «مَلِك» is more far-reaching in praising a creature. The difference between them is that an owner among creatures may not be a king, whereas if Allah the Exalted is King, He is Owner." Ibn al-ʿArabī chose this. [Translator's note: as printed, Abū Ḥātim's statement is listed among arguments for «مَلِك» although it praises «مالِك»; translated as written.] Among them also: that it is more general, since it is annexed to what is owned and what is not owned, unlike «مالك», which is annexed only to what is owned, as stated above; and because it suggests abundance; and because the Exalted praised Himself as Owner of kingship (mulk) in His words: «قل اللَّهُمَّ مالكَ المُلْكِ», and مَلِك is taken from it, as stated above, whereas He did not praise Himself as Owner of ownership (milk) — with kasra on the mīm — from which مالِك is taken.
It has been read مَلْك, with sukūn on the lām, and from this is:
47 - وأيامٍ لنا غُرٍّ طِوالٍ ... عَصَيْنا المَلْكَ فيها أنْ نَدِينا
(And many long, illustrious days of ours, in which we defied the king rather than submit.)
and مَليك, and from this is:
48 - فاقنَعْ بما قَسَم المَليكُ فإنَّما ... قَسَم الخلائِقَ بَيْنَنَا عَلاَّمُها
(So be content with what the King has apportioned, for the One who knows best has apportioned the natures among us.)
and مَلِكي, which is reported from Nāfiʿ.
Once this is known: that «مَلِك» is a naʿt (adjective) of Allah the Exalted is clear, since it is definite through annexation. As for «مالك»: if the past meaning is intended by it, making it a naʿt is also clear, because its annexation is genuine (maḥḍa) and it becomes definite through it. What supports its having a past meaning is the reading of whoever read «مَلَكَ يومَ الدين», making «مَلَك» a past verb. But if the present or future is intended by it, it is problematic, because either it is made a naʿt of Allah — which is not permitted, because the annexation of an active participle with a present or future meaning is not genuine, so it does not become definite, and if it does not become definite it cannot be a naʿt of a definite noun, for what you have learned earlier of the condition of agreement in definiteness and indefiniteness — or it is made a badal, which is weak, because a badal consisting of derived words is rare, as stated above. What ought to be said is that it is a naʿt in the sense that its restriction to a time is not taken into account, because when the described noun is defined by a description, restricting it to a time is not taken into account. So the meaning — and Allah knows best — is that He is characterised as Owner of the Day of Judgement absolutely, without regard to past, present or future. This is what Abū al-Qāsim al-Zamakhsharī inclined toward.
The annexation of مالك and مَلِك to «يوم الدين» is by way of extension (ittisāʿ), since what they relate to is something other than the day; the implied form is: مالكِ الأمرِ كله يومَ الدين ("Owner of the whole affair on the Day of Judgement").
The analogue of the annexation of «مالك» to the adverb of time here is the annexation of «طَبَّاخ» to «ساعات» in the poet's words:
49 - رُبَّ ابنَ عَمِّ لسُلَيْمى مُشْمَعِلّْ ... طَبَّاخِ ساعاتِ الكَرَى زادَ الكَسِلْ
(Many a brisk cousin of Sulaymā, who in the hours of drowsiness cooks the provisions of the lazy.)
except that the object in the verse is mentioned, namely «زادَ الكَسِل», while in the noble verse it is not mentioned, because it is indicated. It is also possible that the speech is taken at face value without assuming any omission.
Attributing ownership (milk) and kingship (mulk) to time in the case of Allah the Exalted is not problematic, and it is supported by the apparent sense of the reading of whoever read «مَلَكَ يومَ الدينِ» as a past verb, for its apparent sense is that «يوم» is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object). The annexation is in the sense of the lām, because that is the basic case. Some of them made it, in this kind of construction, in the sense of «في», relying on the apparent sense of the words of the Exalted: {بَلْ مَكْرُ اليل والنهار} [Sabaʾ: 33]. He said: "The meaning is: plotting in the night, since the night is not described as plotting; only rational beings are described by it, so the plotting takes place in it." The well-known view is that annexation is either in the sense of the lām or in the sense of «مِن», and its being in the sense of «في» is not correct. [Translator's note: the source prints «مَنْ», a misprint for مِن.] As for the words of the Exalted {مَكْرُ اليل}, there is no evidence in them, because this belongs to rhetoric: it is the figurative usage of making their night and their day plotters, as an intensification of how much it occurred from them in both. It is the analogue of their saying: "His day is fasting and his night is standing in prayer", and the poet's words:
50 - أمَّا النهارُ ففي قَيْدٍ وسِلْسِلَةٍ ... والليلُ في قَعْرِ منحوتٍ من السَّاجِ
(As for the day, it is in fetters and a chain; and the night is in the depths of [a box] hewn from teak.)
Since these things frequently occur in these times, they described the times by them as an intensification of that. This is a fine and well-known way in their speech.
Al-yawm (day) linguistically is a portion of time, of whatever time it may be, whether night or daytime. The Exalted said: {والتفت الساق بالساق إلى رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ المساق} [al-Qiyāma: 29–30], which is a metonymy for the dying moments of the dead, and that is not specific to night or daytime. In customary usage, it is from the break of dawn to sunset. Al-Rāghib said: "By al-yawm we express the time from sunrise to its setting." I say: they mentioned this only of al-nahār (daytime), not of al-yawm, and they made the difference between them what I have mentioned to you.
And الدِّيْنِ is likewise a muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct). What is meant by it here is requital (jazāʾ), and from this are the poet's words:
51 - ولم يَبْقَ سوى العُدْوا ... نِ دِنَّاهم كما دَانُوا
(When nothing remained but hostility, we requited them as they had requited.)
i.e. we repaid them as they repaid us. Another said:
52 - واعلَمْ يقيناً أنَّ مُلْكَكَ زائلٌ ... واعلَمْ بأنَّ كما تَدِينُ تُدانُ
(Know for certain that your kingship will pass away, and know that as you requite, you will be requited.)
And similarly:
53 - إذا مل رَمَوْنا رَمَيْناهُم ... ودِنَّاهُمُ مثلَ ما يَقْرِضُونا
(Whenever they shot at us we shot at them, and we repaid them the like of what they lent us.) [Translator's note: «مل» as printed is evidently «ما».]
And similarly:
54 - حَصادُك يوماً ما زَرَعْتَ وإنما ... يُدانُ الفتى يوماً كما هو دائِنُ
(One day you will harvest what you sowed; a young man will one day be repaid as he repays.)
It has other meanings: custom, as in his words:
55 - كَدِينِك من أمِّ الحُوَيْرثِ قبلَها ... وجارتِها أمِّ الرَّباب بِمَأْسَلِ
(As was your custom with Umm al-Ḥuwayrith before her, and her neighbour Umm al-Rabāb, at Maʾsal.)
i.e. like your custom. And similarly:
56 - تقول إذا دَرَأْتُ لها وَضِيني ... أهذا دِينُه أبداً ودِينِي
(She [my she-camel] says, when I fasten her girth for her: Is this always his custom and mine?) [Translator's note: the verse number is printed «5 - 6-» in the source.]
And دانَ means "he disobeyed" and "he obeyed", "he was abased" and "he was mighty", so it is one of the words with opposite meanings (aḍdād). And judgement (qaḍāʾ), from which are the words of the Exalted: {وَلاَ تَأْخُذْكُمْ بِهِمَا رَأْفَةٌ فِي دِينِ الله} [al-Nūr: 2], i.e. in His judgement and ruling. And state (ḥāl): one of the Bedouins was asked [something] and said: "If I were in a state (دِين) other than this, I would have answered you", i.e. in a condition.
And illness (dāʾ), from which are the poet's words:
57 - يا دينَ قلبِك مِن سَلْمى وقد دِينا ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(O the sickness of your heart from Salmā, and it has indeed been made sick …)
One says: دِنْتُه بفعلِه أَدِينُه دَيْناً ودِيناً — with fatḥa or kasra on the dāl in the maṣdar (verbal noun) — i.e. I requited him for his deed. Al-dīn is also obedience, from which is: {وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ دِيناً} [al-Nisāʾ: 125], i.e. in obedience. It is also used metaphorically for the religious community (milla) and the sacred law (sharīʿa). The Exalted said: {أَفَغَيْرَ دِينِ الله يَبْغُونَ} [Āl ʿImrān: 83], meaning Islam, as shown by the words of the Exalted: {وَمَن يَبْتَغِ غَيْرَ الإسلام دِيناً فَلَنْ يُقْبَلَ مِنْهُ} [Āl ʿImrān: 85]. And al-dīn is the conduct of the king. Zuhayr said:
58 - لَئِنْ حَلَلْتَ بجوٍّ في بني أسَدٍ ... في دينِ عمروٍ وحالَتْ بينَنَا فَدَكُ
(If you settle at Jaww among the Banū Asad, under the rule of ʿAmr, with Fadak lying between us …)
One says دِينَ فلان يُدانُ when he is forced into something hateful; from this the slave is called مَدين and the slave-woman مَدِينة. It has also been said: it is from دِنْتُه when you repaid him for his obedience; and some of them placed al-madīna (the city) under this heading. Al-Rāghib said this. The verification of this word will come when it is mentioned.

semin-durr:2-2.t:
Al-ḥamd (praise) is lauding what is beautiful, whether it is a favour bestowed on someone or not. One says: "I praised (حَمِدْتُ) the man for the favour he bestowed on me" and "I praised him for his courage". It is with the tongue alone, without the action of the limbs, since one does not say حَمِدْت زيداً meaning "I did a good deed for him with my hands". This is unlike thanks (al-shukr), which is only for a favour bestowed on another: one says "I thanked him for what he gave me", but one does not say "I thanked him for his courage"; and it is with the heart, the tongue and the limbs. The Exalted said: {اعملوا آلَ دَاوُودَ شُكْراً} [Sabaʾ: 13], and the poet said:
34 - أفادَتْكُمُ النَّعْماءُ مني ثلاثةً ... يدي ولساني والضميرَ المُحَجَّبا
(The favours [you did me] gained you three things from me: my hand, my tongue and my hidden heart.)
[Translator's note: the source prints «الجواح», evidently for الجوارح "the limbs".] So between ḥamd and shukr there is a relation of partial overlap (ʿumūm wa-khuṣūṣ min wajh). It has also been said: al-ḥamd is al-shukr, as shown by their saying: «الحمدُ لله شكراً». It has also been said: between them there is a relation of absolute generality and specificity, al-ḥamd being more general than al-shukr. It has also been said: al-ḥamd is lauding Him, Exalted is He, for His attributes, and al-shukr is lauding Him for His acts; so the one who praises is of two kinds: one who thanks and one who lauds with beautiful attributes. It has also been said: al-ḥamd is a metathesis (maqlūb) of al-madḥ (eulogy). This is not sound, even if it is transmitted from Thaʿlab, because the metathesised form is less used than the form it is metathesised from, while these two are equal in usage, so claiming that one is a metathesis of the other is no more fitting than the reverse; thus they are two independent roots. Also, madḥ cannot be used where ḥamd may be used: one says «حَمِدْتُ الله» but one does not say مَدَحْته; had it been a metathesis, that would not be disallowed. Someone may say: something prevented that, namely the absence of permission for it.
Al-Rāghib said: "Al-ḥamd li-llāh is lauding [Him] for excellence. It is more specific than madḥ and more general than shukr. It is said of what comes from a person by his choice, and [madḥ] of what comes from him and is in him by subjection [i.e. not by his choice]. A person may be eulogised (yumdaḥ) for his tall stature and the beauty of his face, just as he is eulogised for spending his wealth, his courage and his knowledge; but ḥamd is in the second, not the first. And shukr is said only in return for a favour. So every shukr is ḥamd, but not every ḥamd is shukr; and every ḥamd is madḥ, but not every madḥ is ḥamd. One says: فلان محمود when he has been praised; مُحْمَدٌ, [found to be praised]; مُحَمَّد, one whose praiseworthy qualities are many; and أحْمَدُ, i.e. he surpasses others in praise."
As for the alif and lām in «الحَمْد», it has been said that they are for comprehensiveness (istighrāq); it has also been said: for defining the genus (taʿrīf al-jins), and al-Zamakhsharī chose this. The poet said:
35 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... إلى الماجِدِ القَرْمِ الجَوادِ المُحَمَّدِ
(… to the glorious, noble chief, the generous, the much-praised.)
It has also been said: for previous reference (al-ʿahd). Al-Zamakhsharī rejected their being for comprehensiveness and did not explain why. It may be said that what is required of the servant is to perform praise (inshāʾ), not to give information about it; and in that case it is impossible for it to be for comprehensiveness, since the servant cannot perform all praises, from himself and from others — unlike its being for the genus.
Its basic status is that of a maṣdar (verbal noun); for that reason it is not put in the dual or plural. Ibn al-Aʿrābī reported a plural of it on the pattern أَفْعُل and recited:
36 - وأَبْلَجَ محمودِ الثناء خَصَصْتُه ... بأفضلِ أقوالي وأفضلِ أَحْمُدي
(And many a bright-faced man of praiseworthy repute I have singled out with the best of my sayings and the best of my praises.)
The majority read «الحمدُ لِلَّه» with ḍamma on the dāl and kasra on the lām of the preposition. It is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and the khabar (predicate) is the preposition and its genitive noun after it, which is attached (mutaʿalliq) to an omitted word that is in reality the khabar.
Then that omitted word, if you wish, you may assume to be a noun — and this is the preferred view — and if you wish, you may assume it to be a verb; i.e. الحمدُ مستقرٌّ لله ("praise is established for Allah") or استقرَّ لله ("has become established for Allah"). The evidence for preferring the first view is that it is the only possibility in some cases, so there is nothing better to show that it is preferable in the others. That is, when you say «خرجت فإذا في الدار زيدٌ» and «أمَّا في الدار فزيدٌ», in these two cases assuming a noun is the only possibility, because إذا of surprise and أمَّا of detailing can only be followed by a mubtadaʾ. This has been countered by the claim that assuming a verb is the only possibility in some cases, namely when the preposition and its genitive noun is the ṣila (relative clause) of a relative noun, as in «الذي في الدار»; so let it be preferable in the others. The answer is that what we have used for preference belongs to the subject of the mubtadaʾ and khabar and is not foreign to it, so taking it into account is more fitting — unlike its being a ṣila; and the first is not foreign.
A rule must be mentioned here because of its general benefit: when a preposition with its genitive noun, or an adverb (ẓarf), occurs as a ṣila, a ṣifa (adjective), a ḥāl (circumstantial) or a khabar, it is attached to an omitted word, and that omitted word may not appear overtly when it is a general [verb of] being (kawn muṭlaq). As for the poet's words:
37 - لكَ العِزُّ إنْ مَوْلاكَ عَزَّ وإنْ يَهُنْ ... فأنت لدى بُحْبوحَةِ الهُونِ كائِنُ
(Yours is might if your patron is mighty; and if he is abased, then you are in the very midst of abasement.)
it is anomalous and not to be taken into account. As for the words of the Exalted: {فَلَمَّا رَآهُ مُسْتَقِرّاً عِندَهُ} [al-Naml: 40], it was not intended to make the adverb something established, and for that reason the word to which it is attached was mentioned. Then that omitted word may be assumed to be a noun or a verb, except in the ṣila, where it must be a verb, and except in the two cases mentioned, where it must be a noun. They disagreed which of the two assumptions is better outside the excepted cases: some preferred assuming a noun, and some preferred assuming a verb; and the evidence of both parties has already been given.
It has been read, as an anomalous reading, with fatḥa on the dāl of «الحمد». There are two views on it. The more apparent of them is that it is accusative as a maṣdar; then the governing verb was dropped and the maṣdar took its place, as in their saying in statements: «حمداً وشكراً لا كُفْراً» ("praise and thanks, not ingratitude"); the implied form is أَحْمَدُ الله حَمْداً ("I praise Allah with praise"), so it is a maṣdar standing in for a declarative sentence. Al-Ṭabarī said that it contains implicitly His command to His servants to laud Him with it, as if He said: "Say: praise be to Allah"; and on this basis «قولوا إياك» ("say: You [alone] …") comes [later]. On this formulation it would be one of the maṣdars standing in for a request, not a statement. It admits both views, but its being declarative is more fitting than its being a request. This accusative-governing verb may not be made overt, lest the substitute and what it substitutes for be combined. The second view: that it is accusative as a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), i.e. "recite al-ḥamd" or "read al-ḥamd", as in their saying «اللهم ضَبُعاً وذئْباً» ("O Allah, a hyena and a wolf"), i.e. bring together a hyena [and a wolf]. The first is better, because of the verbal indication.
The reading with the nominative is firmer and more eloquent than the reading with the accusative, because the nominative, in the case of maṣdars whose basic function is to stand in for their verbs, indicates permanence and stability, unlike the accusative, which indicates renewal and occurrence. [Translator's note: the source repeats the phrase "unlike the accusative, which indicates permanence and stability" by a copying error before this clause; translated once in its evident sense.] For this reason the scholars said that the answer of the Friend of the Most Merciful [Abraham], peace be upon him, in the words of the Exalted reporting him:
{قَالَ سَلاَمٌ} [Hūd: 69] is better than the words of the angels «قالوا سلاماً», in compliance with the words of the Exalted: {فَحَيُّواْ بِأَحْسَنَ مِنْهَآ} [al-Nisāʾ: 86].
«لله», on the accusative reading, is attached to an omitted word, not to the maṣdar, because it is for clarification (bayān); its implied form is أَعْنِي لله ("I mean: for Allah"), as in their saying سُقْياً له ورَعْياً لك ("watering for him and care for you"), whose implied form is "I mean: for him and for you". What shows that the lām in this type is attached to an omitted word and not to the maṣdar itself is that they did not make the transitive maṣdar govern the word governed by the lām so as to make it accusative and say: سُقياً زيداً or رَعْياً عمراً. This shows that it is not governed by the maṣdar. For that reason whoever made the words of the Exalted {والذين كَفَرُواْ فَتَعْساً لَّهُمْ} [Muḥammad: 8] an instance of ishtighāl (a governing word preoccupied with a pronoun) erred, because «لهم» is not attached to تَعْساً, as stated. It may also be said that the lām in «سُقياً لك» and the like is a strengthening lām for the transitivity of the governing word, since it is secondary [to the verb], so it governs what follows it.
It has also been read with kasra on the dāl. Its justification is that it is a vowel of assimilation (itbāʿ) to the kasra of the lām of the preposition after it. This is the dialect of Tamīm and some of Ghaṭafān: they make the first assimilate to the second for harmony. From this is «اضربِ الساقَيْنُ أُمُّك هابِلُ» ("Strike the two legs, may your mother be bereaved"), with ḍamma on the nūn of the dual because of the ḍamma of the hamza. And similarly:
38 - وَيْلِمِّها في هواءِ الجَوِّ طالبةً ... ولا كهذا الذي في الأرض مطلوبٌ
(Woe to her mother — what a [bird of prey] she is, seeking in the air of the sky! And there is no pursued one like this one on the ground.)
The underlying form is ويلٌ لأُمها. He dropped the first lām, and the ḍamma on the hamza after a kasra was felt heavy, so he transferred it to the lām after stripping it of its vowel and dropped the hamza; then he made the lām assimilate to the mīm, and the word became وَيْلِمِّها. Some do not assimilate, and say وَيْلُمِّها, with ḍamma on the lām. [The poet] said:
39 - وَيْلُمِّها خُلَّةً قد سِيْطَ مِنْ دمِها ... فَجْعٌ وَوَلْعٌ [وإخلافٌ وتَبِدِيلُ]
(Woe to her mother — what a friend she is! Into her blood have been mixed grief-giving, lying, [breaking of promises and fickleness].)
This reading may be from a nominative or from an accusative, because the case-inflection is implied (muqaddar), its appearance being prevented by the vowel of assimilation.
It has also been read «لُلَّهِ», with ḍamma on the lām of the preposition. They said: it is assimilation to the vowel of the dāl. Al-Zamakhsharī preferred it over the reading with kasra on the dāl, giving as the reason that making an indeclinability vowel follow a case-inflection vowel is better than the reverse. It is the dialect of some of Qays: they make the second assimilate to the first, as in مُنْحَدُرٌ and مُقُبلِين, with ḍamma on the dāl and the qāf because of the mīm; and on this basis {مُرْدِفين} [al-Anfāl: 9] has been read with ḍamma on the rāʾ, in assimilation to the mīm. So these are four readings in «الحمدُ لله», and the justification of each of them has been given.
The meaning of the lām of the preposition here is entitlement (istiḥqāq), i.e. praise is due to Allah. It has other meanings which we shall now mention: ownership and entitlement, [as in:] المالُ لزيد ("the wealth belongs to Zayd") and الجُلُّ للفرس ("the saddle-cloth is for the horse"); conferring ownership, as in وَهَبْتُ لك ("I gave to you") and what resembles it, as in {جَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِّنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجاً} [al-Naḥl: 72]; relation, as in لزيد عَمٌّ ("Zayd has a paternal uncle"); causation, as in {لِتَحْكُمَ بَيْنَ الناس} [al-Nisāʾ: 105]; conveying, as in قلتُ لك ("I said to you"); wonder, in oaths specifically, as in his words:
40 - للهِ يَبْقى على الأيام ذو حِيَدٍ ... بمُشْمَخِرٍّ به الظَّيَّانُ والآسُ
(By Allah, there does not survive the days a [mountain goat] with knotted horns on a lofty peak where wild jasmine and myrtle grow.)
clarification (tabyīn), as in the words of the Exalted: {هَيْتَ لَكَ} [Yūsuf: 23]; outcome (ṣayrūra), as in the words of the Exalted: {لِيَكُونَ لَهُمْ عَدُوّاً وَحَزَناً} [al-Qaṣaṣ: 8]; adverbial sense (ẓarfiyya), either meaning "in", as in the words of the Exalted: {وَنَضَعُ الموازين القسط لِيَوْمِ القيامة} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 47], or meaning "at", as in their saying «كتبتُه لخمسٍ», i.e. at five [nights], or meaning "after", as in the words of the Exalted:
{أَقِمِ الصلاة لِدُلُوكِ الشمس} [al-Isrāʾ: 78], i.e. after its declining; termination, as in the words of the Exalted: {كُلٌّ يَجْرِي لأَجَلٍ} [Fāṭir: 13]; and superposition (istiʿlāʾ), as in the words of the Exalted: {وَيَخِرُّونَ لِلأَذْقَانِ} [al-Isrāʾ: 109], i.e. upon their chins. It may also be added (zāʾida) regularly to the object of a verb placed before it, as in the words of the Exalted: {إِن كُنتُمْ لِلرُّؤْيَا تَعْبُرُونَ} [Yūsuf: 43], or when the governing word is secondary, as in the words of the Exalted: {فَعَّالٌ لِّمَا يُرِيدُ} [Hūd: 107]; and irregularly, as in his words:
41 - ولمَّا أَنْ توافَقْنا قليلاً ... أنَخْنا للكلاكِل فارتَمَيْنا
(And when we had met a little while, we made [our camels] kneel on their breasts, and we shot at one another.)
As for the words of the Exalted: {قُلْ عسى أَن يَكُونَ رَدِفَ لَكُم} [al-Naml: 72], it has been said: it is by implication (taḍmīn) [of another verb's meaning]; and it has been said: it is redundant (zāʾida).
His words {رَبِّ العالمين}: al-rabb linguistically is the master, the owner, the one who is established, and the one worshipped; from this is:
42 - أَرَبٌّ يبول الثُّعْلُبان برأسه ... لقد هانَ مَنْ بالَتْ عليه الثعالبُ
(Is it a lord on whose head the male fox urinates? Abased indeed is the one on whom foxes urinate!)
and the one who sets things right. Some added that it means "companion", and recited:
43 - قَدْ ناله ربُّ الكلاب بكفِّه ... بيضٌ رِهافٌ ريشُهُنَّ مُقَزَّعُ
(The master of the dogs reached him with his hand — white, thin [arrows] whose feathers are trimmed.)
The apparent sense is that here it means "owner", so it is not an additional meaning. It has also been said: it may mean "creator".
There is disagreement about it: is it originally an adjective or a maṣdar? Some said: it is an adjective; then these disagreed about its pattern. It has been said: it is on the pattern فَعَل, as when you say نَمَّ يَنُمُّ فهو نَمٌّ ("he slandered, he slanders, so he is a slanderer"). It has also been said: its pattern is فاعِل, its underlying form being رابٌّ; then the alif was dropped because of frequent use, as in their saying رجل بارٌّ and بَرٌّ ("a dutiful man"). Someone may say: we do not concede that بَرّ is taken from بارّ; rather they are two independent forms, so it should not be claimed that ربّ is originally رابّ.
Some said: it is the maṣdar of ربَّهُ يَرُبُّه رَبَّاً, i.e. he owned him. [Someone] said: «لأَنْ يَرُبَّني رجلٌ من قريش أحبُّ إليَّ أن يَرُبِّني رجلٌ من هوازن» ("That a man of Quraysh should be my lord is dearer to me than that a man of Hawāzin should be my lord"). So it is a maṣdar in the sense of the agent, as in رجل عَدْلٌ ("a just man") and صَوم ("fasting"). It is not used of anyone other than the Creator, Exalted is He, except restricted by annexation, as in the words of the Exalted: {ارجع إلى رَبِّكَ} [Yūsuf: 50]; and they say: «هو ربُّ الدار وربُّ البعير» ("he is the owner of the house and the owner of the camel"). The people of the Jāhiliyya used it for a human king without restriction. Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza said:
44 - وهو الربُّ والشهيدُ على يَوْ ... مِ الحِيَارَيْنِ والبلاءُ بلاءُ
(And he is the lord and witness of the Day of al-Ḥiyārayn, and the trial was a [great] trial.)
This was part of their unbelief.
The reading of the majority has it in the genitive as a naʿt (adjective) of «لله» or as a badal (substitute) from it. It has been read in the accusative, and there are three views on it: either [it is accusative] by what al-ḥamd indicates, the implied form being "I praise the Lord of the worlds"; or by cutting it off (qaṭʿ) from following [the preceding noun]; or as a vocative — and this is the weakest of them, because it leads to separating the adjective from the noun it describes. It has also been read in the nominative by cutting it off from following, so it is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "He is the Lord".
Since mention of cutting off from following has come up, let us digress to mention it because of its general benefit. Know that when the described noun is known without its adjective, and the adjective is one of praise, blame or compassion, both following (itbāʿ) and cutting off (qaṭʿ) are permitted in the [following] adjective. Cutting off is either to the accusative by implying a suitable verb, or to the nominative as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ; and neither this accusative-governing verb nor this mubtadaʾ may be made overt. An example is their saying: «الحمدُ لله أهلَ الحمدِ», which is transmitted with «أهل» in the accusative and in the nominative, i.e. "I mean the One worthy of…" or "He is the One worthy of praise".
When adjectives are repeated in this situation, you have the choice between three ways: making all of them follow, cutting all of them off, or cutting some off and making some follow. However, if you make some follow and cut some off, you must begin with following and then bring the cut-off one, not the reverse, as in: مَرَرْتُ بزيد الفاضلِ الكريمُ, lest it entail separating the adjective from the described noun by the cut-off clause.
And العالمين is genitive by annexation; the sign of its genitive is the yāʾ, because it is treated like the sound masculine plural. It is a collective noun (ism jamʿ), because its singular is not from its own word. It cannot be the plural of عالَم, because the correct view regarding «عالَم» is that it is used for everything existent other than the Creator, Exalted is He, as it is derived from al-ʿalāma (sign), in the sense that it points to its Maker; whereas عالَمون in the plural form is used only for rational beings, not others. So it is impossible for عالَمون to be the plural of عالَم, because a plural cannot be more specific than its singular. This is the analogue of what Sībawayh did in holding that «أعراب» is not the plural of «عَرَب», because عَرَب is used of both the desert-dweller and the town-dweller, while أعراب is used only of the desert-dweller, not the town-dweller. If it is said: why may «عالَمون» not be the plural of «عالَم» with the rational being alone intended by it, so that the stated objection disappears? It is answered that, if that were permitted, it would be permitted to say شَيْئون as the plural of شَيء with the rational being alone intended by it; so its not being permitted shows that this cannot be claimed. The answer is open to question, since someone may say: شَيْئون was prevented by another obstacle, namely that it is neither an adjective nor a proper name; so its prohibition does not entail prohibiting «عالَمين» with the rational being intended by it. This is supported by what al-Rāghib transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās: that «عالَمين» was given this plural only because what is meant by it is the angels, the jinn and mankind. Al-Rāghib also said: "Al-ʿālam is originally a name for that by which something is known, just as al-ṭābaʿ (seal) is a name for that with which something is stamped; its structure was put on this form because it is like an instrument, so the world is an instrument in pointing to its Maker." Al-Rāghib also said: "As for its being given the sound plural, that is because human beings are among them, and when a human shares a word with others, his rule prevails." The apparent sense of this is that «عالَمين» is used of rational beings and others, which contradicts what was stated earlier about its being specific to rational beings, as some claimed; and al-Rāghib's statement is the more correct and evident.

semin-durr:7-7.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {صِرَاطَ الذين}: a badal (substitute) from it [i.e. from الصراط المستقيم], a substitute of the whole for the whole; and it is a substitute of a definite from a definite. The badal is of seven kinds, with disagreement about some of them: substitute of the whole for the whole; of part for the whole; of inclusion (ishtimāl); of error (ghalaṭ); of forgetting (nisyān); of change of mind (badāʾ); and of the whole for a part. As for the first three kinds, there is no disagreement about them. As for the substitute of change of mind, some affirmed it, citing as evidence his words, peace be upon him: «إنَّ الرجل ليصلي الصلاةَ، وما كُتب له نصفُها ثلثُها ربعُها إلى العُشْر» ("A man may pray a prayer and there is not recorded for him [of it] its half, its third, its quarter — down to a tenth"); this does not occur in the Quran. As for error and forgetting, some affirmed them, citing the words of Dhū al-Rumma:
72 - لَمْياءُ في شفَتْيها حُوَّةٌ لَعَسٌ ... وفي اللِّثاثِ وفي أَنْيابِها شَنَبُ
(Dark-lipped: on her lips is a darkness — a reddish darkness; and in her gums and her eye-teeth is a sparkling freshness.)
He said: because ḥuwwa is pure blackness, and laʿas is a blackness tinged with red. [Translator's note: i.e. لَعَسٌ is taken as a badal of error from حُوَّةٌ.] These two kinds of substitute do not occur in eloquent speech. As for the substitute of the whole for a part, some affirmed it, citing the apparent sense of his words:
73 - رَحِم اللهُ أَعْظُماً دَفَنُوها ... بسجِسْتَان طَلْحَةَ الطَّلَحاتِ
(May Allah have mercy on bones they buried in Sijistān — Ṭalḥat al-Ṭalaḥāt.)
in the transmission of whoever puts «طلحة» in the accusative. He said: because the bones are part of Ṭalḥa, and Ṭalḥa is the whole, and it has been substituted for them. He also cited for it the words of Imruʾ al-Qays:
74 - كأني غداةَ البَيْنِ يومَ تَحَمَّلوا ... لدى سَمُراتِ الحَيِّ ناقِفُ حَنْظَلِ
(On the morning of parting, the day they loaded up, it was as if I, by the acacias of the tribe, were one splitting colocynth.)
For the morning (ghadāh) is part of the day, and he substituted «اليومَ» for it. There is no proof in the two verses. As for the first: the underlying form is "bones they buried — the bones of Ṭalḥa"; then the muḍāf was dropped and the muḍāf ilayhi was put in its place. What shows this is the well-known transmission, which is with «طلحة» in the genitive, on the basis that the underlying form is أعظُمَ طلحة and he did not put the muḍāf ilayhi in the place of the muḍāf. As for the second: al-yawm is used for a portion of time, as stated earlier. Each of these positions has proofs, objections and answers, whose place is the books of grammar.
It has also been said that the second ṣirāṭ is other than the first, and what is meant by it is knowledge of Allah the Exalted; Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad said this. On this view, its analysis would be that it is conjoined (maʿṭūf) with the conjunction dropped; in any case it is problematic.
The badal is also divided into a substitute of a definite from a definite, an indefinite from an indefinite, a definite from an indefinite and an indefinite from a definite. It is also divided into a substitute of an overt noun from an overt noun, a pronoun from a pronoun, an overt noun from a pronoun and a pronoun from an overt noun. The benefit of the badal is clarification after vagueness, and also that it gives emphasis in meaning, since it is on the intention of repeating the governing word.
And «الذين» is in the position of the genitive by annexation. It is a relative noun because it needs a ṣila (relative clause) and a returning pronoun (ʿāʾid). It is the plural of «الذي» in meaning. The well-known usage is that it is with yāʾ in the nominative, accusative and genitive; some put it in the nominative with wāw, treating it like the sound masculine plural, and from this is:
75 - نحن اللذونَ صَبَّحوا الصَّباحا ... يومَ النُّخَيْلِ غَارةً مِلْحاحَا
(We are the ones who made the morning attack on the day of al-Nukhayl — a relentless raid.)
Its nūn may be dropped because it is lengthened by its ṣila, as in his words:
76 - وإنَّ الذي حَانَتْ بفَلْجٍ دماؤُهُمْ ... هم القومُ كلُّ القومِ يا أمَّ خالدِ
(Those whose blood was shed at Falj are the people — truly the people, O Umm Khālid.)
It is used only of beings endowed with knowledge (rational beings), being treated like the sound masculine plural — unlike its singular, which is used of rational beings and others.
And أَنْعَمْتَ is a verb and its fāʿil (agent), the ṣila of the relative noun. The tāʾ in «أنعمتَ» is the pronoun of the addressee, an attached nominative pronoun. And «عليهم» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أنعمت; the pronoun is the returning pronoun (ʿāʾid), and it is the pronoun of the plural of rational masculines; its attached and detached forms are the same.
The hamza in «أَنْعمت» is for making a thing possess what [the verb] is formed from, so it ought to be transitive by itself; but it was made to imply (ḍummina) the meaning of تفضَّل ("he bestowed favour"), so it takes the same complement as that verb. The pattern أفعل has twenty-four meanings; one has been given, and the rest are: making transitive, as in أخرجته ("I brought him out"); abundance, as in أظبى المكان, i.e. its gazelles became many; becoming, as in أَغَدَّ البعير, it became afflicted with a gland swelling; helping, as in أَحْلَبْتُ فلاناً, i.e. I helped him with milking; privation, as in أَشْكَيْتُه, i.e. I removed his complaint; exposing, as in أَبَعْتُ المتاعَ, i.e. I offered the goods for sale; finding a thing to have the meaning of what [the verb] is formed from, as in أَحْمدته, i.e. I found him praiseworthy; reaching a number, as in أَعْشَرَتِ الدراهم, i.e. they reached ten; or reaching a time, as in أَصْبح ("he entered upon the morning"); or a place, as in أَشْأَمَ ("he reached Syria"); agreeing with the triliteral, as in أَحَزْتُ المكان in the sense of حُزْته ("I took possession of the place"); or dispensing with the triliteral, as in أَرْقَلَ البعير ("the camel went at a quick pace"); muṭāwaʿa (reflexive-resultative) of فَعَل, as in قَشَع الريحُ فَأقْشع السحابُ ("the wind dispersed [the clouds] and the clouds dispersed"); muṭāwaʿa of فَعَّل, as in قَطَّرْته فَأَقْطَرَ; negation of the instinct, as in أَسْرع [Translator's note: so printed («نفي الغزيرة»); the example أسرع does not obviously fit, and the phrase may be corrupt]; naming, as in أخْطَأْتُه, i.e. I called him mistaken; supplication, as in أَسْقيته, i.e. I said to him: "May Allah give you water"; being due, as in أَحْصَدَ الزرعُ, i.e. the crop became due for harvest; arriving, as in أَعْقَلْته, i.e. I made my intellect reach him; facing, as in أفَفْتُه, i.e. I faced him with my saying "uff"; bringing a thing, as in أكثرتُ, i.e. I brought much; distinguishing between أَفْعَل and فَعَل, as in أشرقت الشمس, it shone, and شَرَقَتْ, it rose; and coming upon suddenly, as in أَطْلَعْتُ على القوم, i.e. I came upon the people. [Translator's note: the source counts twenty-four meanings, but fewer are listed here.]
And «على» is a particle of superposition (istiʿlāʾ), literal or figurative, as in عليه دَيْنٌ ("a debt is upon him"). It has other meanings, among them: passing beyond (mujāwaza), as in his words:
77 - إذا رَضِيَتْ عليَّ بنو قُشَيْر ... لَعَمْرُ الله أعجبني رضاها
(When the Banū Qushayr are pleased with me — by the life of Allah, their pleasure delights me.)
i.e. عني ("with me"); in the sense of the bāʾ: {حَقِيقٌ عَلَى أَنْ لاَّ أَقُولَ} [al-Aʿrāf: 105], i.e. بأَنْ; in the sense of «في»: {مَا تَتْلُواْ الشياطين على مُلْكِ سُلَيْمَانَ} [al-Baqara: 102], i.e. in the reign [of Solomon]; accompaniment, as in {وَآتَى المال على حُبِّهِ ذَوِي القربى} [al-Baqara: 177]; causation, as in {وَلِتُكَبِّرُواْ الله على مَا هَدَاكُمْ} [al-Baqara: 185], i.e. because of His guiding you; in the sense of «مِنْ»: {حَافِظُونَ * إِلاَّ على أَزْوَاجِهِمْ} [al-Muʾminūn: 5–6], i.e. except from their wives; and redundancy, as in his words:
78 - أبى الله إلاَّ أنَّ سَرْحَةَ مالكٍ ... على كلِّ أَفْنانِ العِضاهِ تَرُوقُ
(Allah has willed nothing but that Mālik's tall tree should surpass all the branches of the thorn-trees.)
because «تروق» is transitive by itself. Each of these places is open to examination.
It hovers between being a particle and a noun. It is a noun in two places. The first: when a preposition comes before it, as in his words:
79 - غَدَتْ مِنْ عليه بعد ما تَمَّ ظِمْؤُها ... تَصِلُ وعن قَيْضٍ بزَيْزَاءَ مَجْهَلِ
(She [the sand-grouse] set off from upon it [the egg], after her thirst-interval was complete, rattling [with thirst], and from eggshells on a trackless hard ground.)
and its meaning is the meaning of «فوق», i.e. from above it. The second: when making it a particle would lead to a verb whose agent is a pronoun being made transitive to its own attached pronoun outside the places where that is permitted, as in his words:
80 - هَوِّنْ عليكَ فإنَّ الأمورَ ... بكفِّ الإِلهِ مقاديرُها
(Take it easy upon yourself, for the measures of all affairs are in the hand of God.)
Like it in these two rules is «عَنْ», which will come, if Allah the Exalted wills.
Some claimed that «على» hovers between noun, verb and particle. The noun and the particle have been dealt with; as for the verb, he said: you say «علا زيدٌ», i.e. he rose high. This is open to question, because «على» when it is a verb is derived from al-ʿuluww (height), whereas when it is a noun or particle it has no derivation, so it is not the same thing. However, this speaker would rebut this objection by their saying that خَلا and عدا hover between being verbs and particles, and they did not pay attention to this objection.
The basic vowel of the hāʾ of the pronoun is ḍamma. If a vowelless yāʾ or a kasra precedes it, those other than the people of the Ḥijāz give it kasra, as in عَلَيْهِم, فيهم and بهم. The well-known usage for its mīm is sukūn before a vowelled letter and kasra before a vowelless letter — this is when you give the hāʾ kasra; but if you give it ḍamma, kasra [on the mīm] is not permitted except under poetic necessity, as in his words: «وفيهُمِ الحكام», with kasra on the mīm.
In «عليهم» there are ten dialectal forms, some of which have been read: عليهِمْ [with kasra on] the hāʾ, and with ḍamma on it, with sukūn on the mīm; عليهِمي; عَلَيْهُمُ; عليهِمُو, with kasra on the hāʾ and ḍamma on the mīm with an added wāw; عليهُمي, with ḍamma on the hāʾ and an added yāʾ after the mīm, or with kasra only; عليِهِمُ, with kasra on the hāʾ and ḍamma on the mīm. Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī mentioned this. [Translator's note: the list as printed is defective and does not reach ten forms; translated as written.]
And «غيرِ» is a badal from «الذين», a substitute of an indefinite from a definite. It has also been said: a naʿt (adjective) of الذين, which is problematic, because «غير» is indefinite and «الذين» is definite. They gave two answers to this. The first: «غير» is indefinite only when it does not occur between two opposites; when it occurs between two opposites, the otherness is confined, so «غير» then becomes definite by annexation. You say: مررتُ بالحركة غير «السكون» ("I passed by motion, other than rest"), and the verse is of this kind. This works only on the view of Ibn al-Sarrāj, and it is the weaker view. The second: the relative noun resembles indefinites in the vagueness it contains, so it was treated as an indefinite. It has also been said: «غير» is a badal from the genitive pronoun in «عليهم». This is problematic on the view of those who hold that the badal takes the place of what it substitutes for and that the first is intended to be discarded, since it would entail the ṣila being void of a returning pronoun — do you not see that the implied form would become: صراطَ الذين أنعمت على غيرِ المغضوبِ عليهم?
And «المغضوب» is genitive by annexation. It is a passive participle, and what stands in place of the agent (nāʾib fāʿil) is the preposition and its genitive noun. So the first «عليهم» is in the position of the accusative and the second in the position of the nominative. The al in it is relative, the implied form being غيرِ الذين غُضِبَ عليهم ("other than those against whom there is anger"). The correct view about relative al is that it is a noun, not a particle.
Know that the word «غير» is always singular and masculine; however, if a feminine is intended by it, the verb predicated of it may be made feminine. You say: قامت غيرُك ("someone other than you stood up"), meaning a woman. It is originally an adjective in the sense of the active participle, namely مغاير ("different"); for this reason it does not become definite by annexation, and likewise its sisters, I mean words like مثل, شِبْه, شبيه, خِدْن and تِرْب. It may be used for exception, by analogy with «إلاّ», just as إلاّ may be used as an adjective by analogy with it. It may also be meant as negation, like لا, so that the object of what it governs may be placed before it, just as is permitted with «لا». You say: أنا زيداً غيرُ ضاربٍ ("I am not one to strike Zayd"), i.e. غير ضاربٍ زيداً; and from this are the poet's words:
81 - إنَّ امرأً خَصَّني عَمْداً مودَّتَه ... على التنائي لَعِنْدي غيرُ مَكْفورِ
(A man who deliberately singled me out for his affection despite the distance — with me he is surely not met with ingratitude.)
Its implied form is لغيرُ مكفورٍ عندي. This is not permitted with it when it is not for negation: if you said جاء القومُ زيداً غيرَ ضاربٍ, meaning غيرَ ضاربٍ زيداً, it would not be permitted, because it is not in the sense of «لا», with which that is permitted according to the correct view regarding «لا». There is a second view on it which forbids that absolutely, and a third view distinguishing between its being the answer to an oath, in which case it is not permitted, and its not being so, in which case it is permitted.
It is one of the words that are always annexed, overtly or in implication; so putting the alif and lām on it is a mistake.
It has been read «غيرَ» in the accusative. It has been said: it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «الذين». This is weak, because it comes from the muḍāf ilayhi outside the places where that is permitted, as you will learn, if Allah the Exalted wills. It has been said: from the pronoun in «عليهم». And it has been said: as a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ). Al-Farrāʾ rejected this; he said: because «لا» is added only when a negation precedes it, as in his words:
82 - ما كان يرضى رسولُ الله فِعْلَهما ... والطيبان أبو بكرٍ ولا عُمَرُ
(The Messenger of Allah would not have approved of what they did, nor the two good ones, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.)
They answered that «لا» is a redundant connective (ṣila zāʾida), like it in the words of the Exalted: {مَا مَنَعَكَ أَلاَّ تَسْجُدَ} [al-Aʿrāf: 12], and the poet's words:
83 - وما ألومُ البيضَ ألاَّ تَسْخَرا ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(And I do not blame the fair women for mocking …)
and the words of another:
84 - وَيلْحَيْنَني في اللهو ألاَّ أُحِبُّه ... وللَّهوِ داعٍ دائبٌ غيرُ غافلِ
(They reproach me about amusement, that I love it — and amusement has a constant caller who never neglects.)
and the words of another:
85 - أبى جودُه لا البخلَ واستعجلتْ نَعَمْ ... به مِنْ فتىً لا يمنعُ الجودَ نائِلُه
(His generosity refused "no" — stinginess — and "yes" hastened with him, from a young man whose gift does not withhold generosity.)
So «لا» in these places is a redundant connective. This answer is open to question, because al-Farrāʾ did not say that it is not redundant; so their saying that «لا» is redundant in this verse and their likening it to the preceding places is of no use. The correct formulation of the answer is that they should say: «لا» has been found redundant without a preceding negation, as in these preceding places. It is also possible that «لا» in his words «لا البخلَ» is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) of «أبى», and that «البخلَ» is accusative as a badal from «لا», i.e. his generosity refused the saying of "no", and saying "no" is stinginess. This is supported by his words «واستعجَلَتْ به نَعَمْ», where he made «نَعَم» the fāʿil of «استعجَلَتْ»; so it is a case of verbal predication (isnād lafẓī), i.e. his generosity refused this word, and this [other] word hastened with him.
It has also been said: the accusative of «غيرَ» is by implying أعني ("I mean"); this is reported from al-Khalīl. Some assumed something omitted after «غير»; he said: the implied form is غيرَ صراطِ المغضوبِ ("other than the path of those against whom there is anger"). He stated this assumption without restriction, not tying it to the genitive or accusative of «غير», but it only works with its accusative, and it would be an adjective of His words {الصراط المستقيم}. This is weak, because whenever a badal and an adjective come together, the adjective is put first. So it is better that it be an adjective of «صراطَ الذين». It may be a badal from {الصراط المستقيم} or from {صِرَاطَ الذين}, but that entails repetition of the badal, and its permissibility is open to question; there is no transmitted ruling on the matter, except that they have mentioned it in the substitute of change of mind specifically. Or [it may be] a ḥāl from the first or the second «الصراط».
Know that wherever we make «غير» an adjective, it is necessary to hold either that «غير» is definite or that the described noun is vague and treated as an indefinite, as was set out above for the reading with «غير» in the genitive.
And «لا» in His words {وَلاَ الضآلين} is redundant (zāʾida), to reinforce the meaning of negation understood from «غير», lest it be imagined that «الضالِّين» is conjoined with {الذين أَنْعَمْتَ}. The Kufans said: it is in the sense of «غير». This is close to its being redundant, for if «غير» were stated explicitly, it too would be for emphasis; and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb read it so [i.e. وغير الضالين].
And «الضَّالين» is genitive, conjoined with «المغضوب». It has been read, as an anomalous reading: الضَّأَلِّين, with the alif turned into hamza. They recited:
86 - وللأرضِ أمَّا سُودُها فَتَجلَّلَتْ ... بياضاً وأمَّا بِيضُها فادْهََأمَّتِ
(And as for the earth: its dark parts were covered with white, and its white parts turned dark.)
Abū al-Qāsim al-Zamakhsharī said: "They did that out of zeal in fleeing from the meeting of two vowelless letters." End of quote. But they have done that where there are not two vowelless letters. The poet said:
87 - فخِنْدِفٌ هامةُ هذا العَألَمِ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Khindif is the head of this world …)
with hamza in «العَأْلَمِ». Another said:
88 - ولَّى نَعامُ بني صفوانَ زَوْزَأَةً ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(The ostriches of the Banū Ṣafwān turned away, running with a waddling gait …)
with hamza in place of the alif of «زَوْزأة». The apparent conclusion is that it is a regular dialect, for they said about the reading of Ibn Dhakwān «مِنْسَأْتَه», with a vowelless hamza, that its original is an alif which was changed into a vowelless hamza.
If it is said: why did He make the ṣila of الذين a past verb? It is said: to indicate the established and realised nature of Allah's bestowal of favour upon them. And He made the ṣila of al a noun so that it would include all times. And He made it passive to make the expression beautiful, because it does not befit the One from whom guidance is sought and to whom bestowal of favour is attributed that anger be attributed to Him, since this is a situation of gentleness and courtesy in seeking kindness, so it is not fitting to address Him with an attribute of vengeance.
Al-inʿām is conveying kindness to another, and it is said only when the one to whom kindness is conveyed is a rational being; so one does not say: "So-and-so bestowed favour on his horse" or "his donkey".
Al-ghaḍab (anger) is the surging of the blood of the heart out of desire for vengeance; from this is his saying, peace be upon him: «اتقوا الغضبَ فإنه جَمْرةٌ تُوقَدُ في قلب ابن آدم، ألم تَرَوْا إلى انتفاخ أَوْداجه وحُمْرةِ عينيه» ("Beware of anger, for it is an ember kindled in the heart of the son of Adam; have you not seen the swelling of his jugular veins and the redness of his eyes?"). When the Creator, Exalted is He, is described by it, what is meant is vengeance and nothing else. One says: فلانٌ غَضَبة when he is quick to anger.
One says: غضِبت لفلانٍ ("I was angry for so-and-so") [when he is alive], and غضبت به when he is dead. It has also been said: anger is the change of the heart because of something disliked. It has also been said: if punishment is meant by anger, it is an attribute of action; and if the will to punish is meant by it, it is an attribute of essence.
Al-ḍalāl is being hidden and absent; it has also been said: perishing. From the first is their saying: ضَلَّ الماءُ في اللبن ("the water was lost in the milk"), and his words:
89 - ألم تسأَلْ فَتُخْبِرَكَ الدِّيارُ ... عن الحيِّ المُضَلَّلِ أين ساروا
(Did you not ask — so that the abodes might tell you — about the tribe that was lost to sight, where they went?)
And al-ḍalḍala is a smooth stone that the torrent rolls back and forth in the valley. From the second is: {أَإِذَا ضَلَلْنَا فِي الأرض} [al-Sajda: 10]. It has also been said: al-ḍalāl is deviating from the straight path. It may also be used to express forgetting, as in the words of the Exalted: {أَن تَضِلَّ إْحْدَاهُمَا} [al-Baqara: 282], as shown by His words: {فَتُذَكِّرَ}.
The discussion of «آمين»: it is not part of the Quran, by consensus. Its meaning is "Answer!" So it is a verbal noun (ism fiʿl) indeclinable on fatḥa. It has also been said: it is not a verbal noun; rather, it is one of the names of the Creator, Exalted is He, the implied form being "O Āmīn". Abū al-Baqāʾ declared this weak for two reasons. The first: if it were so, it ought to be indeclinable on ḍamma, because it would be a singular, definite noun addressed in the vocative. The second: the names of Allah the Exalted are fixed by revelation (tawqīfiyya). Al-Fārisī justified the view of whoever made it a name of Allah the Exalted in the sense that it contains a pronoun referring to Allah the Exalted, because it is a verbal noun. This is a good justification; the author of «al-Mughrib» transmitted it.
There are two dialectal forms of āmīn: with the long vowel and with the short. From the first are his words:
90 - آمينَ آمينَ لا أرضى بواحدةٍ ... حتى أُبَلِّغَهَا ألفينِ آمينا
(Āmīn, āmīn! I will not be content with one until I bring it to two thousand āmīns.)
Another said:
91 - يا رَبِّ لا تَسْلُبَنِّي حُبَّها أبداً ... ويَرْحمُ اللهُ عبداً قال آمينا
(O Lord, never strip me of her love — and may Allah have mercy on a servant who says āmīn.)
And from the second are his words:
92 - تباعَدَ عني فُطْحُلٌ إذ دعوتُه ... آمينَ فزاد الله ما بيننا بُعْدا
(Fuṭḥul drew away from me when I called him — amīn! May Allah increase the distance between us.)
It has also been said: the long form is a foreign noun, because it has the measure of Qābīl and Hābīl. Is doubling the mīm permitted? The well-known view is that it is a mistake; al-Jawharī transmitted this. But doubling has been reported from al-Ḥasan and Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq, and it is the view of al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl, [taking it] from أمَّ, when one makes for something, i.e. "we are making toward You"; and from this is {ولا آمِّينَ البيت الحرام} [al-Māʾida: 2].

semin-durr:1-1.t:
[Translator's note: the entry begins mid-discussion; the word being explained is «البسملة» (al-basmala, saying "In the name of Allah").] It is the maṣdar (verbal noun) of «بَسْمَلَ», i.e. he said: «بسم الله», like «حَوْقَلَ», «هيْلَلَ» and «حَمْدَلَ», i.e. he said: «لا حول ولا قوة إلا بالله», «لا إله إلا الله» and «الحمد لله». This resembles the chapter of naḥt (blending) in relational adjectives (nisba): that is, they take two nouns, carve a single word out of them, and form the relational adjective from it, as in their saying «حَضْرَميّ», «عَبْقَسيّ» and «عَبْشَميّ», relating to Ḥaḍramawt, ʿAbd al-Qays and ʿAbd Shams. The poet said:
6 - وتضحَكُ مني شَيْخَةٌ عَبْشَمِيَّة ... كَأَنْ لم تَرَيْ قبلي أسيراً يَمانياً
(An old woman of ʿAbd Shams laughs at me, as though you had never before seen a Yemeni captive.)
It is not regular (ghayr maqīs); so, no wonder that some said of «بَسْمل» and «هَيْلل» that they are a post-classical (muwallad) usage. [Al-Māwardī said: one who says «بسم الله» is called «مُبَسْمِل», and it is] a post-classical usage, though it has occurred in poetry; ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa said:
7 - لقد بَسْمَلَتْ ليلى غداةَ لقِيتُها ... ألا حَبَّذا ذاكَ الحديثُ المُبَسْمِلُ
