(Laylā said "bismillāh" on the morning I met her; how excellent is that basmala-uttering talk!)
Others among the lexicographers reported it without saying that it is post-classical, such as Thaʿlab and al-Muṭarriz.

«وبِسْم»: a preposition and its genitive noun. The bāʾ here is for istiʿāna (seeking aid / instrument), as in «عَمِلت وبالقَدُوم» ("I worked with the adze") [Translator's note: the «و» before «بالقدوم» appears to be a misprint; the example is «عملتُ بالقَدوم».], because the meaning is: I recite seeking aid by Allah. It has other meanings which we promised earlier to mention, namely:
- ilṣāq (adhesion), literal or figurative, as in: «مَسَحْتُ برأسي» ("I wiped my head"), «مررْتُ بزيدٍ» ("I passed by Zayd");
- causation (sababiyya), [as in] {فَبِظُلْمٍ مِّنَ الذين هَادُواْ حَرَّمْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ} [al-Nisāʾ: 160], i.e. because of their wrongdoing;
- accompaniment (muṣāḥaba), as in: «خرج زيدٌ بثيابه» ("Zayd went out with his clothes"), i.e. accompanied by them;
- substitution (badal), as in his saying ﷺ: «ما يَسُرُّنِي بها حُمْرُ النَّعَم» ("Red camels in exchange for it would not please me"), i.e. in place of it, and as in the saying of another:
8 - فليتَ لي بِهِمُ قوماً إذا ركبوا ... شَنُّوا الإِغارةَ فرساناً ورُكْبانا
(Would that I had, in place of them, a people who, when they mount, launch the raid as horsemen and camel-riders.)
i.e. in place of them;
- the oath: «أحلفُ باللهِ لأفعلنَّ» ("I swear by Allah I shall surely do it");
- location (ẓarfiyya), as in: «زيد بمكة» ("Zayd is in Mecca"), i.e. in it;
- transitivisation (taʿdiya), as in: {ذَهَبَ الله بِنُورِهِمْ} [al-Baqara: 17];
- partition (tabʿīḍ), as in the poet's saying:
9 - شَرِبْنَ بماءِ البحر ثم ترفَّعَتْ ... متى لُجَجٍ خُضْرٍ لهنَّ نَئيجُ
(They drank of the sea's water, then rose up from green deep waves, with a roaring sound.)
i.e. of its water;
- exchange (muqābala): «اشتريتهُ بألف» ("I bought it for a thousand"), i.e. I matched it with this price;
- mujāwaza (meaning "from / about"), as in His saying, Exalted is He: {وَيَوْمَ تَشَقَّقُ السمآء بالغمام} [al-Furqān: 25], i.e. from the clouds. Some said: it is so only with asking in particular, as in: {فَاسْأَلْ بِهِ خَبِيراً} [al-Furqān: 59], i.e. about Him, and the saying of ʿAlqama:
10 - فإنْ تَسْأَلوني بالنساءِ فإنني ... خبيرٌ بأَدْواءِ النساء طبيبُ
إذا شابَ رأسُ المرءِ أو قلَّ مالُه ... فليس له في وُدِّهِنَّ نَصيبُ
(If you ask me about women, I am expert in women's ailments, a physician: when a man's head turns grey or his wealth dwindles, he has no share in their affection.)
- istiʿlāʾ (superiority, "upon"), as in His saying, Exalted is He: {مَنْ إِن تَأْمَنْهُ بِقِنْطَارٍ} [Āl ʿImrān: 75].
The majority refuse to make it anything but ilṣāq or taʿdiya, and they reduce all the places mentioned to these two; but this is not the place for arguing and resolving.

It may be added (zāʾida, redundant), regularly and irregularly. Regularly: on the fāʿil (agent) of «كفى», as in: {وكفى بالله} [al-Nisāʾ: 6], i.e. Allah suffices, as is shown by its dropping in the poet's saying:
11 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... كفى الشيبُ والإِسلامُ للمرءِ ناهياً
(Grey hair and Islam suffice as a restrainer for a man.)
And on the khabar (predicate) of «ليس» and of its sister «ما» when not made affirmative by «إلاَّ», as in His saying, Exalted is He: {أَلَيْسَ الله بِكَافٍ [عَبْدَهُ]} [al-Zumar: 36], {وَمَا رَبُّكَ بِغَافِلٍ} [al-Anʿām: 132]; and in: «بحَسْبكِ زيدٌ». Irregularly: on the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) of «كفَى», as in his saying:
12 - فكفى بنا فَضْلاً على مَنْ غيرُنا ... حُبُّ النبيِّ محمدٍ إيانا
(It suffices us as merit over those other than us that the Prophet Muḥammad loves us.)
i.e. «كَفانا»; and there is other discussion about this verse. And on the mubtadaʾ (subject) other than «حَسْب»; from this, according to one of two views, is: {بِأَييِّكُمُ المفتون} [al-Qalam: 6]; but it was also said that «المفتون» is a maṣdar like «المَعْقول» and «المَيْسور», and on this view it is not redundant. And on the khabar of «لا», the sister of «ليس», as in his saying:
13 - فكُنْ لي شفيعاً يومَ لا ذو شفاعةٍ ... بمُغْنٍ فتيلاً عن سَوادِ بنِ قاربِ
(So be an intercessor for me on the day when no one possessing intercession will avail Sawād ibn Qārib a whit.)
i.e. «مُغْنياً». And on the khabar of «كان» when negated, as in:
14 - وإنْ مُدَّتِ الأيدي إلى الزادِ لم أكنْ ... بِأعجلِهم، إذْ أَجْشَعُ القومِ أَعْجَلُ
(When hands are stretched out to the provisions, I am not the hastiest of them, since the greediest of people is the hastiest.)
i.e. «لم أكنْ أعجلَهم». And on the ḥāl (circumstantial) and on the second of the two objects of «ظنَّ», when these are also negated, as in his saying:
15 - فما رَجَعَتْ بخَائِبَةٍ رِكابٌ ... حكيمُ بنُ المُسَيَّب مُنْتَهاها
(No riding camels whose destination is Ḥakīm ibn al-Musayyab have come back disappointed.)
and the saying of another:
16 - دعاني أخي والخيلُ بيني وبينه ... فلمَّا دعاني لم يَجِدْني بقُعْدَدِ
(My brother called me while the horses were between me and him; when he called me, he did not find me a coward who holds back.)
i.e. «ما رَجَعَت رِكابُ خائبةً» and «لم يَجِدْني قُعْدَداً». And on the khabar of «إنَّ», as in the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
17 - فإنْ تَنْأَ عنها حِقْبَةً لا تُلاقِها ... فإنك ممَّا أَحْدَثَتْ بالمُجَرِّبِ
(If you stay far from her for a long time without meeting her, you are indeed one who has tried what she has done.)
i.e. «فإنك المجرِّب»; and in: {أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْاْ أَنَّ الله} [al-Aḥqāf: 33] and the like.

«الاسم» (the noun / name), lexically: that which makes clear a thing named. Technically: that which indicates a meaning in itself only, not touching by its form upon a time, and no part of which indicates a part of its meaning; by this last restriction the nominal sentence is excluded. «التسمية» (naming) is making that word indicate that meaning.

People have disagreed: is the name identical with the thing named or other than it? It is a long question, about which people have spoken in early and later times. Against its being the thing named they objected that it is annexed to it, which would entail annexing a thing to itself. Abū al-Baqāʾ answered this with three answers, the best of which is: that «الاسم» here means naming (tasmiya), and naming is other than the name, because naming is uttering the name, while the name is what adheres to the thing named, so they differ. The second: that there is an omitted muḍāf in the speech, its implied form being «باسم مُسَمَّى اللهِ» ("in the name of the one named Allah"). The third: that the word «اسم» is redundant, as in his saying:
18 - إلى الحَوْلِ ثم اسمُ السلامِ عليكما ... ومَنْ يَبْكِ حولاً كاملاً فقد اعتذَرْ
(Until a year has passed; then the name of peace be upon you both; whoever weeps a full year has done his duty.)
i.e. «السلام عليكما», and the saying of Dhū al-Rumma:
19 - لاَ يَرْفَعُ الطرفَ إلاَّ ما تَخَوَّنَهُ ... داعٍ يُناديه باسمِ الماءِ مَبْغَومُ
(It does not raise its eye except when a caller visits it from time to time, calling it with the name of water, a bleating cry.)
This was the view of Abū ʿUbayda, al-Akhfash and Quṭrub.
They differed over the meaning of this redundancy. Al-Akhfash said: "So that it passes out of the status of an oath to the intent of seeking blessing." Quṭrub said: "It was added for reverence and magnification." These two answers are weak, because redundancy and omission are resorted to only when one is compelled to them.

Of this same kind — I mean what gives the impression of annexing a thing to itself — is the annexation of the name to the nickname (laqab) and of the qualified noun to its adjective, as in: «سعيدُ كُرزٍ», «زيدُ قُفَّةٍ», «مسجدُ الجامعِ» and «بَقْلَةُ الحمقاءِ». But the grammarians interpreted the first type by making the name mean the thing named and the nickname mean the word, so its implied form is: "the one named by this word came to me"; and the second they took as involving an omitted muḍāf, so the implied form of «بقلةِ الحمقاءِ» is «بقلةُ الحبِّةِ الحمقاءِ», and of «مسجدُ الجامعِ», «مسجدُ المكانِ الجامعِ».

The grammarians differed over its derivation. The Basrans held that it is derived from «السُّمُوّ», which is elevation, because it indicates the thing named, raising it and making it manifest. The Kufans held that it is derived from «الوَسْم», which is a mark, because it is a mark of the thing named. This, though sound in meaning, is unsound in morphology (taṣrīf).
The Basrans argued for their view from their broken plural of it as «أَسْماء» and its diminutive as «سُمَيّ», since the broken plural and the diminutive return things to their roots; and the Arabs say: «فلانٌ سَمِيُّك» ("so-and-so is your namesake"), «سَمَّيْتُ فلاناً بكذا» and «أَسْمَيْتُه بكذا». This shows its derivation from «السموّ». Had it been from «الوَسْم», one would say in the plural «أَوْسام», in the diminutive «وُسَيْم», and they would say «وَسِيمُك فلانٌ», «وَسَمْتُ» and «أَوْسَمْتُ فلاناً بكذا»; their not saying this shows that it is not so. Further, making it from «السموّ» puts it in the more common category, while making it from «الوَسْم» puts it in the less common category; for omission of the lām (the third radical) is frequent and omission of the fāʾ (the first radical) is rare. Further, we have found that they usually compensate in a place other than that of the omission, so making the hamzat al-waṣl (connective hamza) a compensation for the lām agrees with this principle, unlike claiming that it compensates for the fāʾ.
If it is said: their saying «أسماء» in the plural and «سُمَيّ» in the diminutive has no probative force, since the root form could be «أَوْساماً» and «وُسَيْماً», after which the word was metathesised by moving its fāʾ after its lām, so that «أَوْسام» became «أَسْماواً» and then underwent the same weakening as «كساء», and «وُسَيْم» became «سُمَيْوَاً» and then underwent the weakening of «جُرَيّ», the diminutive of «جَرْو» — the answer is that claiming this is of no use, because metathesis (qalb) is contrary to rule, so it is not resorted to unless necessity calls for it.
Does this disagreement have any consequence or not? The answer is that it does: whoever says it is derived from elevation (al-ʿuluww) says that He has never ceased to be qualified [by His names] before the existence of creation, after them and at their extinction; they have no effect on His names or attributes — and this is the view of Ahl al-Sunna. Whoever says it is derived from «الوَسْم» says that Allah in pre-eternity was without name or attribute, and when He created creation they assigned Him names and attributes — and this is the view of the Muʿtazila; it is a graver error than their saying that the Quran is created. On this disagreement also rests the disagreement about the name and the thing named.

There are five dialectal forms of «الاسم»: «اسم» with ḍamma and with kasra on the hamza, and «سُِم» with kasra and with ḍamma on the sīn. [Translator's note: the source lists four forms here; the fifth, «سُمًى», is given below.] Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā [Thaʿlab] said: "«سُمٌ» with ḍamma on the sīn takes it from «سَمَوْتُ أسْمُو», and whoever says it with kasra takes it from «سَمَيْتُ أَسْمي»." On the two forms is his saying:
20 - وعامُنا أَعْجبنا مُقَدَّمُهْ ... يُدْعى أبا السَّمْحِ وقِرضابٌ سُِمُهْ
مُبْتَرِكاً لكلِّ عَظْمٍ يَلْحُمُهْ
(Our leader, whose forefront pleased us, is called Abū al-Samḥ, and Qirḍāb is his name, bent over every bone, stripping its flesh.)
It is recited both ways. And they cited for the kasra:
21 - باسمِ الذي في كلِّ سورةٍ سِمُهْ
(In the name of Him whose name is in every sūra.)
[On this, there are two views concerning the lām of «اسم»: one, that it is wāw; the second, that it is yāʾ — and this is strange; but] Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā is of great standing and trustworthy in what he reports. And «سُمَىً», like «هُدَىً». They argued for it from the poet's saying:
22 - واللهُ أَسْماك سُمَىً مُبارَكاً ... آثرك اللهُ به إيثارَكَا
(Allah has named you with a blessed name, by which Allah has preferred you with His preference.)
But there is no proof in this, since it may be from the dialect of those who make it a defective noun (manqūṣ) with ḍamma on the sīn and brought it in the accusative; it would only stand as proof if «سُمَىً» were said in the nominative or genitive.

Its hamza is a hamzat al-waṣl, i.e. it is retained at the start of speech and dropped in continuous speech; it may be retained by poetic necessity, as in his saying:
23 - وما أنا بالمَخْسوسِ في جِذْمِ مالكٍ ... ولا مَنْ تسمَّى ثم يلتزِم الإِسْما
(I am not one of base descent in the stock of Mālik, nor one who takes a name and then clings to the name [alone].)
It is one of the ten nouns begun with a hamzat al-waṣl, namely: «اسم», «است», «ابن», «ابنُم», «ابنة», «امرؤ», «امرأة», «اثنان», «اثنتان» and «ايمنُ» in the oath. The rule for this hamza is that it be written, like other connective hamzas; they dropped it only when the noun is annexed to the Name of Majesty in particular, owing to frequent use. It was also said: so that the writing matches the pronunciation. And it was said: there is no omission at all, because the root form is «سِمٌ» or «سُم», with kasra or ḍamma on the sīn; when the bāʾ came onto it, the ʿayn (the sīn) was made quiescent for lightness, because a kasra or ḍamma came after a kasra. [Al-Naḥḥās reported this, and it is good.] If it is annexed to something other than the Name of Majesty, it is retained, as in «باسم الرحمن»; this is the well-known view. It is reported from al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash that it may be dropped when annexed to names of the Creator, Exalted is He, other than the Name of Majesty, as in «بسمِ ربِّك», «بسمِ الخالق».

Know that every preposition with its genitive noun must have something to which it is attached (mutaʿalliq): a verb or what carries a verb's meaning — except in three cases: the redundant preposition, and «لعلَّ» and «لولا» for those who put the genitive after them. Ustādh Ibn ʿUṣfūr added the kāf of comparison, but that amounts to nothing, for it is attached. This being established, «بسم الله» must have something to which it is attached, but it has been omitted.
The grammarians differed about this. The Basrans held that what it is attached to is a noun; the Kufans held that it is a verb. Then each of the two parties differed among themselves. Some of the Basrans held that this omitted element is a mubtadaʾ, omitted together with its khabar, with its governed element remaining, its implied form being: «ابتدائي باسم الله كائنٌ أو مستقرٌ» ("my beginning in the name of Allah is existing / established"), or «قراءتي باسم الله كائنةٌ أو مستقرة» ("my recitation in the name of Allah is …"). This is open to question, since it entails omitting the maṣdar while keeping what it governs, which is not allowed; Makkī expressly ruled out this view. Others held that it is a khabar omitted together with its mubtadaʾ, its governed element remaining and standing in its place, the implied form being: «ابتدائي كائنٌ باسمِ الله» or «قراءتي كائنةٌ باسم الله», as in «زيدٌ بمكةَ». On the first view it is in the position of the accusative; on the second, in the position of the nominative, because it stands in place of the khabar.
Some of the Kufans held that this omitted verb is implied before it, saying: because the default is to put [the verb] first; the implied form is «أقرأُ باسم الله» ("I recite in the name of Allah") or «أبتدئُ باسم الله» ("I begin in the name of Allah"). Others implied it after it: «باسم الله أقرأ» or «أبتدئ» or «أتلو». Al-Zamakhsharī inclined to this; he said: "So that the fronting conveys restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ), because it came as a rebuttal of the unbelievers who used to begin with the names of their gods, saying: 'In the name of al-Lāt, in the name of al-ʿUzzā'." This is very good. He then raised against himself His saying, Exalted is He: {اقرأ باسم رَبِّكَ} [al-Qalam: 1] [Translator's note: the verse is al-ʿAlaq 96:1; the source labels it al-Qalam, a name sometimes given to this sūra.], where this governing word is stated explicitly before what it governs, and he answered that fronting the verb in Sūrat al-ʿAlaq is more fitting, because it is the first sūra revealed, so the command to recite was more important. Others answered that «باسم ربك» is attached not to the «اقرأ» before it but to the «اقرأ» after it, so it conforms to the aforementioned rule.
This is open to question, because on this view the apparent sense is that the second «اقرأ» is a tawkīd (emphasis) of the first, so the governed element of the emphasising word would have separated it from what it emphasises, in addition to the separation by a long stretch of speech.
They also differed: is that verb an imperative or a statement? Al-Farrāʾ held that it is an imperative, its implied form being: «اقرأ أنت باسم الله» ("recite, you, in the name of Allah"). Al-Zajjāj held that it is a statement, its implied form being: «اقرأ أنا» [Translator's note: so in the source; the intended form is presumably «أقرأ أنا», "I recite".] or «أبتَدِئُ» and the like.

«الله» in «بسم الله» is a muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct). Is what governs the muḍāf ilayhi the muḍāf, an implied preposition, or the meaning of annexation? There are three views, the best of which is the middle one. It is a proper name (ʿalam) of the One truly worshipped; it is applied to no other, and no created being has dared to take it as a name. Likewise «الإِله», before the transfer [of the hamza's vowel] and the assimilation, is applied only to the One truly worshipped. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is as if it became a proper name by predominance (bi-l-ghalaba)." As for «إله» without the alif and lām, it is applied to the One truly worshipped and to others; He, Exalted is He, said: {لَوْ كَانَ فِيهِمَآ آلِهَةٌ إِلاَّ الله لَفَسَدَتَا} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 22], {وَمَن يَدْعُ مَعَ الله إِلَهَا آخَرَ لاَ بُرْهَانَ لَهُ بِهِ} [al-Muʾminūn: 117], {[أَرَأَيْتَ] مَنِ اتخذ إلهه هَوَاهُ} [al-Furqān: 43].
People differed whether it is murtajal (coined, underived) or derived; the correct view is the first, and it is the most definite of definite nouns. It is related that Sībawayh was seen in a dream and was asked: "What did Allah do with you?" He said: "Much good, because I made His name the most definite of definites."
Then those who hold that it is derived differed greatly. Some said: it is derived from «لاهَ يليه», i.e. to be elevated; hence the sun was called «إلاَهة», with kasra and with fatḥa on the hamza, because of its elevation — or, it was said, because they took it as an object of worship. On this basis it was said «لَهْيَ أبوك», meaning «للهِ أبوك», the ʿayn having been moved to the place of the lām; and he lightened it by dropping the alif and lām and dropping the preposition. Some went far and made from this the poet's saying:
24 - ألا ياسَنا بَرْقٍ على قُلَلِ الحِمى ... لَهِنَّكَ من برقٍ عليَّ كريمُ
(O gleam of lightning over the peaks of al-Ḥimā, by Allah, you are a lightning dear to me!)
He said: the root form is «لله إنك كريمٌ عليَّ»; the preposition, the definite article and the alif before the hāʾ of the Name of Majesty were dropped, the hāʾ was made quiescent, treating continuous speech like a pause, so the word became «لَهْ»; then the vowel of the hamza of «إنَّ» was thrown onto the hāʾ, leaving «لَهِنَّك», as you see. This is an ugliness on the part of the one who said it; there are two views on the verse easier than this.
Some said: "It is derived from «لاه يَلُوه لِياهاً», i.e. to be veiled." On these two views the alif is radical, so the root of the word is «لاَهَ»; then the definite article came onto it, giving «اللاه»; then the lām of the article was assimilated into the following lām, since the conditions of assimilation were met, and its lām was given the heavy (velarised) pronunciation (tafkhīm). Its pattern on the two preceding views is either faʿal or faʿil, with fatḥa or kasra on the ʿayn; on every supposition the weak letter was vowelled and preceded by a fatḥa, so it was changed into alif; the root form was «لَيَهاً», «لَيِهاً», «لَوَهاً» or «لَوِهاً».
Some made it derived from «أَلَه». «أَلَه» is a word shared among several meanings: worship, finding repose, bewilderment and resorting in fear. So the meaning of «إله» is that His creation worship Him, find repose in Him, are bewildered about Him and resort to Him in fear. From it is the saying of Ruʾba:
25 - لِلَّهِ دَرُّ الغانِياتِ المُدَّهِ ... سَبَّحْنَ واسْتَرْجَعْنَ مِنْ تألُّهي
(How excellent are the praising fair maidens! They said "subḥān Allah" and "innā li-llāh" at my devotion.)
i.e. at his worship; and from it is {وَيَذَرَكَ وَآلِهَتَكَ} [al-Aʿrāf: 127], i.e. your worship. The Commander of the Faithful alluded to the meaning of bewilderment in his saying: "The embellishment of descriptions falls short before His attributes, and the turns of language go astray there." That is because when the servant reflects on His attributes he is bewildered; hence it is related: "Reflect on the bounties of Allah, and do not reflect on Allah." On this view the hamza is radical and the alif before the hāʾ is extra, so the root of the noble Name of Majesty is «الإِله», as in the poet's saying:
26 - معاذَ الإِله أن تكونَ كظبيةٍ ... ولا دُمْيَةٍ ولا عَقِيْلَةٍ رَبْرَبِ
(God forbid that she should be like a gazelle, or a statue, or the choicest of a herd of wild cows.)
Then the hamza was dropped owing to frequent use, as it was dropped in «ناس», whose root is «أُناس», as in his saying:
27 - إنَّ المَنايا يَطَّلِعْ ... نَ على الأُناس الآمِنينا
(The fates come suddenly upon people who feel secure.)
So the [lām of the] definite article met the lām, was assimilated into it, and was given tafkhīm. Or we say: the hamza of «الإِله» was dropped by transfer (naql), meaning that we transferred its vowel to the lām of the article and dropped it after transferring its vowel, as is known in naql; then the lām of the article was assimilated, as has been mentioned, except that the transfer here is obligatory owing to frequent use.
Some said: it is derived from «وَلِهَ», since every created being is yearning (wālih) towards Him; on this basis one of the sages said: "Allah is beloved of all things," and this is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: {وَإِن مِّن شَيْءٍ إِلاَّ يُسَبِّحُ بِحَمْدَهِ} [al-Isrāʾ: 44]. Its root form is «وِلاه»; then the wāw was changed into hamza, as it was changed in «إشاح» and «إعاء», whose roots are «وِشاح» and «وِعاء»; so the word became «إلاهاً», and then what was described above was done to it: dropping its hamza and assimilation. This view is attributed to al-Khalīl. On these two [latter] views the pattern of «إلاه» is fiʿāl, in the sense of mafʿūl (passive participle), i.e. worshipped, or one about whom people are bewildered, like «الكِتاب» in the sense of «مكتوب».
Al-Khalīl's view was rejected on two grounds. First: if the hamza were a substitute for wāw, it would be permissible to pronounce the original, yet no one has said it, whereas they say «إشاح» and «وشاح», «إعاء» and «وعاء». Second: if it were so, it would be pluralised as «أَوْلِهة», like «أَوْعِية» and «أَوشِحَة», with the hamza returned to its original; yet «إله» is pluralised only as «آلهة».
Al-Khalīl can get clear of these two objections by [saying] that the substitution became binding in this noun because it is distinguished by rules in which nothing else shares, as you will see; and then the plural came following the binding substitution.

As for the alif and lām, the discussion of them depends on whether it is derived or not. If the first is held, they were originally the definite article; if the second, they are extra. Their dropping from the Name of Majesty is anomalous in their saying «لاهِ أبوك», whose root is «للهِ أبوك», as mentioned. They said: the alif before the hāʾ was dropped in writing so that it would not resemble the writing of «اللات», the name of the idol, because some change this tāʾ into hāʾ in pause and write it with hāʾ following the pause; hence the resemblance would arise.
It was also said: so that it would not resemble the writing of «اللاه», the active participle of «لها يلهو» (to amuse oneself). This holds only in the dialect of those who drop the yāʾ of the definite defective noun in pause, since writing follows it; but for those who retain it in pause and so retain it in writing, there is no confusion. It was also said: dropping the alif is a rare dialectal usage on which the writing was based, and this was made binding owing to its frequent use. The poet said:
28 - أقبلَ سَيْلٌ كان من أمر اللهْ ... يَحْرِدُ حَرْدَ الجَنَّة المُغِلَّهْ
(A flood came on, from the command of Allah, making for the fruitful garden with determined intent.)
The rule for its lām is tafkhīm, out of reverence, unless preceded by a kasra, in which case it is pronounced light (tarqīq) — even though Abū al-Qāsim al-Zamakhsharī stated tafkhīm without qualification, but he means what I have said. Abū al-Baqāʾ reported that some pronounce it light in every case; this amounts to nothing, because the Arabs, generation after generation, are against it, as al-Zamakhsharī mentioned. The scholars of the readings reported a disagreement where it is preceded by a fatḥa with imāla, i.e. close to kasra: some pronounce it light and some heavy, as in the reading of al-Sūsī in one of his two ways: «حتى نَرَى اللهَ جَهْرةً».
Al-Suhaylī and Ibn al-ʿArabī reported a strange view about it: that the alif and lām in it are radical, not extra; they excused the connective nature of the hamza by frequent use, as al-Khalīl says about the hamza of the definite article. Their view was rejected on the ground that the Name of Majesty would then have to take tanwīn, since its pattern would be faʿʿāl, like «لآَّل» and «سَآَّل», and there is nothing in it to prevent tanwīn; this shows that «أل» in it is extra to the essence of the word.
Among the strange things reported about it as well is that it is not Arabic but Arabicised, of Syriac origin, its root being «لاها», which the Arabs Arabicised, saying «الله». They argued for this from the poet's saying:
29 - كحَلْفَةٍ من أبي رياحِ ... يَسْمَعُها لاهُهُ الكُبارُ
(Like an oath from Abū Riyāḥ, which his great god hears.)
So he brought it in the original form before Arabicisation. Abū Zayd al-Balkhī reported this.
[Among the strange things reported about it as well is that its root is the hāʾ which is the pronoun for the absent one.] They said: that is because they affirmed Him as existing in the view of their intellects, so they pointed to Him with the pronoun; then the lām of possession was added to it, since they knew that He is the Creator and Owner of things, so the word became «لَهُ»; then the alif and lām were added for reverence and magnification. This does not resemble the speech of the lexicographers or the grammarians; it resembles only the speech of some Sufis.
Among the strange things reported about it as well is that it is an adjective, not a noun. The one who held this argued that a name makes the thing named known, while Allah, Exalted is He, is not perceived by the senses nor by intuition, so His name does not make Him known — only His attributes make Him known; and because a proper name stands in place of pointing, and that is impossible in His case, Exalted is He. Al-Zamakhsharī rejected this view with words meaning that you describe it but do not describe with it: you say «إله عظيم واحد» ("a great, one God"), as you say «شيءٌ عظيم» and «رجلٌ كريم», but you do not say «شيء إله», just as you do not say «شيء رجل»; were it an adjective, it would occur as an adjective of something else, not as a qualified noun. Further, His beautiful attributes must have a qualified noun to which they apply; if you made all of them adjectives, they would remain not applied to any noun qualified by them. And there is no disagreement about anything other than the Name of Majesty being an adjective; so it is settled that the Name of Majesty is a noun, not an adjective.
The discussion of this noble name admits of more length than I have mentioned to you; I abridged it only for fear of wearying the reader of this book.

«الرحمن الرحيم»: two adjectives derived from «الرحمة» (mercy). It was also said: «الرحمن» is not derived, because the Arabs did not know it, in their saying: {وَمَا الرحمن} [al-Furqān: 60]. Ibn al-ʿArabī answered this by [saying] that they were ignorant of the attribute, not of the One it qualifies; that is why they did not say: «ومَنْ الرحمن» ("and who is al-Raḥmān?"). The two follow the noun they qualify in four of the ten [things] mentioned. [Translator's note: this refers to the ten features (case, definiteness, number, gender, etc.) in four of which a naʿt agrees with its noun, as set out earlier in the author's introduction.]
Al-Aʿlam al-Shantamarī held that «الرحمن» is a badal (substitute) for the name Allah, not a naʿt (adjective) of it; this rests on his view that «الرحمن» is a proper name by predominance. He argued for this from its occurring without following a qualified noun, as in His saying, Exalted is He: {الرحمن عَلَّمَ القرآن} [al-Raḥmān: 1-2], {الرحمن عَلَى العرش استوى} [Ṭā Hā: 5]. Al-Suhaylī rejected this, [saying] that were it a badal it would clarify what precedes it, while what precedes it — the Name of Majesty — needs no clarification, since it is the most definite of proper names; do you not see that they said {وَمَا الرحمن} [al-Furqān: 60] and did not say «وما اللهُ»? End of quotation. As for his saying "it occurred without following [a noun]", that does not prevent its being an adjective, because when the qualified noun is known it may be omitted with its adjective remaining, as in His saying, Exalted is He: {وَمِنَ الناس والدوآب والأنعام مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ} [Fāṭir: 28], i.e. a kind differing [in colours], and as in the poet's saying:
30 - كناطحٍ صخرةً يوماً لِيُوْهِنَها ... فلم يَضِرْها وأَوْهَى قرنَه الوَعِلُ
(Like one who butts a rock one day to weaken it, but does not harm it — the mountain goat only weakened its own horn.)
i.e. like a butting mountain goat; and this is frequent.

«الرحمة», lexically, is tenderness and inclining [towards another]; from it is derived «الرَّحِم» (the womb), which is the belly [Translator's note: the source reads «الابطن», apparently a misprint, perhaps for «البطن» (the belly).], because it inclines over the foetus. On this basis, His being described, Exalted is He, by mercy is a figurative expression (majāz) for His bestowing favours on His servants, like a king who, when he inclines towards his subjects, his good reaches them. This is the meaning of the words of Abū al-Qāsim al-Zamakhsharī. On this supposition it is an attribute of action, not an attribute of essence. It was also said: mercy is willing good for whomever Allah wills that for; on this view describing Him by it is literal (ḥaqīqa), and it is then an attribute of essence. This view is the apparent one.
It was also said: mercy is a tenderness that entails doing good to the one shown mercy; it is used sometimes for mere tenderness and sometimes for mere doing good; when the Creator, Exalted is He, is described by it, nothing is meant but mere doing good, without tenderness. On this basis it is related: "Mercy from Allah is bestowal of favour and bounty, and from human beings it is tenderness and sympathy."
[Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "They are two tender names, one of them more tender than the other," i.e. more abundant in mercy. Al-Khaṭṭābī said: this is problematic, because tenderness] has no place among His attributes. Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl said: "This is an error of the narrator; rather they are two gentle names (rafīqān), one of them gentler than the other, and gentleness (al-rifq) is one of His attributes." And he ﷺ said: "Allah is Gentle and loves gentleness, and gives for it what He does not give for harshness"; and the ḥadīth supports it. As for «الرحيم», it is the One gentle towards the believers in particular.

The scholars differed about «الرحمن الرحيم» as to whether they have one meaning or different meanings.
Some held that they have one meaning, like «نَدْمان» and «نَدِيم» (boon companion). These then differed on two views. Some said: they were combined for emphasis. Others said: when Musaylima — may Allah curse him — named himself «الرحمن», Allah said of Himself: «الرحمنُ الرحيم», so the combination of these two attributes belongs to Allah, Exalted is He, alone. This is very weak, for his naming himself thus counts for nothing at all; and also «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم» preceded the appearance of Musaylima's affair.
Others said: each one has a benefit other than the benefit of the other, and they made this relate to the difference in what each is connected to, since it is said: "Raḥmān of this world and Raḥīm of the Hereafter" — this is related from the Prophet ﷺ — because His mercy in this world embraces believer and unbeliever, while in the Hereafter it is particular to the believers. It is also related: "Raḥīm of this world and Raḥmān of the Hereafter." Distinguishing between them by this measure alone is open to a question that is not hidden.
Others held that the two are different; and these too differed. Some said: «الرحمن» is more intensive, and therefore it is not applied to any but the Creator, Exalted is He. Al-Zamakhsharī chose this and placed it in the category of «غَضْبان» and «سَكْران», for one filled with anger and drunkenness; hence it is said: "Raḥmān of this world and the Hereafter, and Raḥīm of the Hereafter only." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "So the rule would have been to rise from the lower to the higher, as one says «شُجاع باسل» ('brave, intrepid') and does not say «باسِلٌ شجاع»." Then he answered that He followed «الرحمن», which covers the great favours and their roots, with «الرحيم», to be like a completion and a sequel covering the fine and subtle among them.
Others reversed this and made «الرحيم» more intensive. This is supported by the narration of whoever said: "Raḥīm of this world and Ḥamān [sic] of the Hereafter" [Translator's note: «وحمان» in the source is evidently a misprint for «ورحمان».], because in this world He has mercy on believer and unbeliever, while in the Hereafter He has mercy only on the believer. But the correct view is that «الرحمن» is more intensive. As for this narration, there is no proof in it; rather it indicates that «الرحمن» is more intensive, because on the Day of Resurrection mercy is manifold greater and its effect more manifest, according to what is related: that He has stored up for His servants ninety-nine mercies for the Day of Resurrection. The apparent view is that the aspect of intensiveness in the two differs: the intensiveness of faʿlān is from the aspect of fullness and predominance, and the intensiveness of faʿīl is from the aspect of repetition and occurrence at the places of mercy. Abū ʿUbayda said: "The form faʿlān is not like the form faʿīl, for the form faʿlān occurs only for intensiveness of the action, as in «رجل غَضْبانُ», for one filled with anger; while faʿīl may be in the sense of the active and of the passive [participle]." He said:
31 - فأمَّا إذا عَضَّتْ بك الحربُ عَضَّةً ... فإنك مَعْطوفٌ عليك رحيمُ
(But when war bites you with a bite, you are one who is shown sympathy, pitied.)
So «الرحمن» is particular in name and general in action, and «الرحيم» is general in name and particular in action; therefore faʿlān does not take a direct object, while faʿīl does. Ibn Sīdah reported: «زيدٌ حفيظٌ علمَك وعلمَ غيرك» ("Zayd retains your knowledge and the knowledge of others").

The alif and lām in «الرحمن» are for predominance (ghalaba), as in «الصَّعِق». According to most scholars it is not applied to any other than the Creator, Exalted is He, because of His saying, Exalted is He: {قُلِ ادعوا الله أَوِ ادعوا الرحمن} [al-Isrāʾ: 110], where He set it as an equivalent to that in which there is no sharing — unlike «رحيم», which is applied to others than Him, Exalted is He; He [the Exalted] said concerning the Prophet ﷺ:
{بالمؤمنين رؤوف رحيم} [al-Tawba: 128]. As for the saying of the poet about Musaylima the Liar — may Allah the Exalted curse him:
32 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... وأنت غَيْثُ الوَرى لا زلت رَحْمانا
(And you are the rain [succour] of mankind; may you never cease to be raḥmān.)
no attention is paid to his saying, owing to the excess of their obstinacy. It is used only made definite by the alif and lām or annexed; and no attention is paid to his saying «لا زِلْتَ رَحْمانا», because of its anomaly.
Among the strange things reported about it is that it is Arabicised, not Arabic in origin, and that it is [originally] with the dotted khāʾ; Thaʿlab [and al-Mubarrad] said this, [and he recited]:
33 - لن تُدْرِكوا المَجْدَ أو تَشْرُوا عَباءَكُمُ ... بِالخَزِّ أو تَجْعلوا اليَنْبُوتَ ضَمْرانا
أو تَتْرُكونَ إلى القَسَّيْنِ هِجْرَتَكُمْ ... ومَسْحكم صُلبَهم رَخْمانَ قُرْبانا
(You will not attain glory until you exchange your woollen cloaks for silk, or turn the carob shrub into ḍamrān [a fragrant plant], or abandon your migration to the two priests and your stroking of their cross as an offering to Rakhmān.)

Regarding joining «الرحيم» to «الحمد» there are three ways. The one followed by the majority: «الرحيمِ» with kasra on the mīm, joined to «الحمد». In this kasra there are two possibilities: one — and it is the sounder — that it is a case vowel (ḥarakat iʿrāb); and it was said: it is possible that the mīm was made quiescent with the intention of pausing, and when a quiescent letter came after it, it was vowelled with kasra. The second of the ways of joining: making the mīm quiescent and pausing on it, then beginning with the alif of «الحمد» pronounced as a disjunctive hamza; Umm Salama related this from him ﷺ. The third: al-Kisāʾī reported from some of the Arabs that they recite: «الرحيمَ الحمدُ», with fatḥa on the mīm and joining the alif of «الحمد», as if they made it quiescent and pronounced the alif disjunctively, then treated the pause like continuous speech and threw the vowel of the connective hamza onto the quiescent mīm. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This has not been transmitted as a reading from anyone [as far as I know]," and this is open to a question that will come at {الم الله} [Āl ʿImrān: 1-2]. I say: its verification will come in Āl ʿImrān, if Allah the Exalted wills. This admits of another interpretation, namely that the vowel is for the accusative by an omitted verb, by way of qaṭʿ (cutting off [the adjective from its noun]) — and that is preferable to this strained explanation.
